Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Auxiliary and Detail Views

Show a flat sloping surface straight on, enlarge a small region, or shorten a long part on the sheet.

Extra views make sloping surfaces and small features easier to read

Extra views make sloping surfaces and small features easier to read

An auxiliary view is an extra drawing view that looks straight at a flat, sloping surface so its shape is clear. A tilted rectangular surface can look shortened from above; looking straight at it reveals its rectangular proportions.

A detail view is an enlarged picture of a selected small region, such as a hole with crowded edges or dimensions. The actual part stays the same size. Use an auxiliary when the viewing direction makes the shape hard to read, and a detail when a small region needs more room.

A view's scale tells you how large its picture is compared with the real part. Read the view labels and scale information to connect an added view to the original drawing. To expose an interior hidden behind solid material, use a section view.

Look perpendicular to a face to see its true shape

Look perpendicular to a face to see its true shape

A face is a surface on the part. Look straight at a flat face, perpendicular to it, to see its true shape. In projection terms, that face is parallel to the imaginary flat surface on which the view is drawn: the projection plane.

In the figure, the part is a wedge with a flat, sloping rectangular face. The front view sees that face edge-on, so the face is reduced to the line P–Q. The light-blue rectangle is the same face viewed straight on in the auxiliary view.

In this example, the front view sees the inclined face on edge. The top view shows it foreshortened: its sloping length appears shorter because the view is not looking straight at the face. The top view's 160-unit length is not the face's true 200-unit length.

Scale is the ratio of a length on the drawing to its actual length. “True shape” still allows the stated drawing scale; it does not mean the image must be life size. The auxiliary view shows the face's correct proportions without the shortening caused by the viewing direction.

A primary auxiliary view is constructed directly from a principal view, such as the front, top, or side. Choose its projection plane parallel to the inclined face. Review Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box and Choosing Drawing Views for the principal views.

Supporting detail: Addendum 1 — When one auxiliary view is not enough.

A detail enlarges a feature; a break shortens the view

A detail enlarges a feature; a break shortens the view

The existing view from which a detail is taken is its parent view. A boundary and letter usually identify the selected region. In the figure, the circle marked B locates the region shown in Detail B.

Match the detail label and read its scale. 2:1 means a drawn length is twice the actual length; the hole itself has not grown. Enlargement alone does not change the viewing direction or reveal hidden features.

A broken view omits a middle length of a long, substantially uniform part so its ends and features fit on the sheet. Break lines identify the omission. The actual part remains continuous, and dimensions across the break state its full size. Use those dimensions rather than measuring the shortened illustration.

A broken view is different from a broken-out section, which shows interior geometry by representing a local portion of material as removed. See Section Views.

Project from the edge view and transfer the missing depth

Project from the edge view and transfer the missing depth

The auxiliary figure above uses the front view as its parent. Its thin projectors are construction lines used to line up corresponding points in the two views.

  1. Find the principal view in which the face is a line. In the example, the front view shows the sloping face edge P–Q.
  2. Draw a fold or reference line parallel to P–Q. It represents the hinge between the parent and auxiliary projection planes.
  3. Draw thin projectors perpendicular to the fold line from the face’s corners.
  4. Transfer each corner’s depth from the corresponding principal view, using the same reference and drawing scale. Here the top view supplies a constant depth of 80.
  5. Connect corresponding points. The face is a 200-by-80 rectangle in the auxiliary view, although the top view shows its sloping length shortened to 160.

These are invented drawing units for the construction. The projectors and fold line are not physical edges on the part. The auxiliary view shows this face's true shape, not necessarily the true shape of every other face.

Use a partial auxiliary view when only one face matters

Use a partial auxiliary view when only one face matters

A partial auxiliary view shows the useful inclined face and enough nearby geometry to identify it. Omit unrelated geometry that would make the view crowded, using an appropriate break boundary where the view is interrupted.

Keep the viewing reference, label, and scale clear. Partial means limited coverage; it does not change the projection direction. The construction above isolates the inclined face for that reason.

Create auxiliary, detail, and break views from the parent in CAD; Practice

Create auxiliary, detail, and break views from the parent in CAD

Auxiliary view
Select the parent and a reference edge representing the inclined face edge-on. Use Auxiliary View in SOLIDWORKS or Auxiliary view in Onshape, check the direction, and place the view. For a partial view, limit the displayed region with the application’s crop or partial-view controls while retaining identifying references.
Detail view
Use Detail View in SOLIDWORKS or Detail view in Onshape. Define the region, place the enlarged view, and set its scale and label. Verify that dimensions reference the intended model edges.
Broken view
Use Break View in SOLIDWORKS or Break view in Onshape. Choose break direction and style, then position the two break boundaries. Check that no feature needed to define the part was omitted.

Review the result after every model revision. A generated view can be geometrically valid yet omit the feature the reader needs.

Supporting detail: Addendum 2 — Vendor help and dimensioning references.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Choosing Drawing Views

Use flat views from different directions, with dimensions and notes, to describe a part clearly.

Drawing views describe one part from different directions

Drawing views describe one part from different directions

A drawing view is a flat picture of a part seen from one direction. A set of views, read together with dimensions and notes, describes one three-dimensional part so someone can make or inspect it.

A front view shows width and height. Looking from above or from the side can show the front-to-back depth that the front leaves out. In this stepped-block example, the front explains the step heights, while the top shows how far the block extends back.

Choosing views means selecting the directions that explain the shape clearly. Orthographic Projection explains how the views line up and how their positions tell you the viewing direction.

Choose the front view that explains the shape

Choose the front view that explains the shape

The front view is a drawing of the part from the direction chosen as the starting point for the other views. The side shown need not be the one that happened to face you when you picked up the part.

Start with a stable, understandable orientation. Prefer a view that shows characteristic shapes directly and keeps important features out of hidden lines, the dashed lines used for edges blocked from sight. For a stepped part, a profile that shows the steps is usually more useful than a plain rectangle.

The front, top, and side are principal views: views along the part's main directions. Once the front is chosen, the other principal views follow from it. Keep their orientation and alignment consistent with Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box.

One or two views can be enough when the missing information is stated

One or two views can be enough when the missing information is stated

One view
A flat plate with a constant thickness can be defined by its face view and a thickness note, provided the outline, holes, and other requirements are completely specified. A circle alone does not say whether the part is a disk, a sphere, or a cylinder.
Two views
A constant-depth stepped shape can use a profile and a top view to establish the step widths, heights, and front-to-back depth. A third view may add no new information. A simple cylindrical part can often be described with a side view and an end view.
Three views
Front, top, and a side view are useful when features change across all three directions. Each view should resolve a question the others leave open.

Three is a common arrangement, not a quota. Dimensions, notes, symmetry, and repeated geometry can supply information without drawing every side. The remaining views and written requirements must still define the whole part.

Add a view when it removes a real ambiguity

Add a view when it removes a real ambiguity

A view is useful when it answers a question the existing views leave open. For example, the same circular front outline could belong to a thin disk or a long cylinder. A side view or a length note can resolve that difference. If two different parts still fit the drawing, identify the missing information and add the view or written callout that separates them.

Hidden interior
A section view can expose a bore or recess more clearly than a tangle of dashed lines. Its cutting-plane arrows tell you which way to look.
Flat sloping surface
An auxiliary view looks straight at the surface from an extra direction so its shape is clear. Another front, top, or side view may still make it appear shortened. See Auxiliary and Detail Views for that construction.
Small feature
An enlarged detail view makes a crowded feature readable. Read its stated scale; do not compare its apparent size directly with the main view.

Supporting detail: Addendum 3 — Why more pictures do not automatically mean more information.

Check the view set before moving on to dimensions; Checklist; Practice

Check the view set before moving on to dimensions

  • Confirm that the front view exposes the most useful shape.
  • Account for width, height, and depth without guessing.
  • Locate every hole, step, slot, or recess in enough views to explain its direction and extent.
  • Check hidden edges and the projection convention for consistency.
  • Remove a redundant view only if the remaining views and callouts still define the part.

Then continue to Drawing Dimensioning for placing the size and location information. Use Measurement Language for units and Tolerances and Fits for permitted variation.

Practice choosing a view set

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Drawing Terminology Review

Recognize drawing terms used when turning a drawing into a CAD model, then follow links for the full methods.

Identify the view before interpreting the shape

Identify the view before interpreting the shape

This short vocabulary review supports CAD certification preparation. It is general drawing language, not a list of guaranteed exam terms.

A view is a picture of the part from a chosen direction. First identify how the picture represents the part; then read its lines, dimensions, and notes.

Orthographic view
The principal orthographic views look straight at the part from the front, above, or a side, using parallel lines of sight perpendicular to each viewing plane. Front shows width and height; top shows width and depth; a side view shows depth and height. Read the views together to understand one three-dimensional part.
Isometric view
An angled pictorial that helps you see width, height, and depth together. Its three principal axis directions are 120° apart and use the same scale. An isometric projection foreshortens lengths equally along all three axes; an ordinary isometric drawing lays out axis-parallel lengths at the chosen drawing scale. Use stated dimensions to model the part rather than measuring its apparent lengths on the picture.
Line conventions describe edges and centers within a view

Line conventions describe edges and centers within a view

A view type tells you how the part is represented. A line convention tells you what a particular mark means within that view. Visible, hidden, and center lines are line conventions, not additional view types.

Visible line
A continuous line shows an edge or outline you can see from this viewing direction.
Hidden line
Short dashes show an edge concealed by material.
Center line
A long-short pattern identifies an axis, center, or symmetry reference. It is not a physical seam in the part.
Read dimensions and callouts as instructions about features; Practice

Read dimensions and callouts as instructions about features

Dimension and extension lines
A dimension gives a size or location. A dimension line is a thin line, usually ending in arrowheads, that shows the extent of the measurement; extension lines carry the edges of the measured feature out to it. Read the value and units instead of measuring a picture. See Dimension Anatomy and Placement.
Diameter and radius
Diameter spans a circle through its center; radius runs from its center to its edge. The diameter symbol is Ø; R denotes radius. Confusing them changes the modeled size. See how holes and arcs are called out in Hole and Feature Callouts.
Hole and feature callout
A note describing a feature, possibly including quantity, size, depth, or thread information. A through hole passes through the material; a blind hole stops within it. See Hole and Feature Callouts.
Tolerance
The permitted variation in a specified dimension. Read the stated limits or applicable drawing note; do not assume that every dimension has the same tolerance. See Dimension Anatomy and Placement.

Practise radius and diameter

Distinguish a section, a detail, and an auxiliary view; Practice

Distinguish a section, a detail, and an auxiliary view

  • Section view: shows the part as if cut by an imaginary plane so internal features can be read. A cutting-plane indication locates the cut; section lining identifies material crossed by it. See Section Views.
  • Detail view: enlarges a selected area so small features are easier to read. Check its scale and labels.
  • Auxiliary view: looks perpendicular to an inclined surface to show its true shape. Compare it with a detail view in Auxiliary and Detail Views.

Before modeling, point to the view or callout that establishes each feature. If a shape is unclear, look for another view rather than guessing from a pictorial.

Check the purpose of a detail view

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Engineering Graphics in the Design Process

Use sketches to explore ideas, models to develop geometry, and drawings to communicate a design for making and checking.

Choose a graphic for the question you need to answer; Practice

Choose a graphic for the question you need to answer

Engineering graphics communicate technical ideas and problem solutions. Aim for accuracy, simplicity, and clarity. A graphic succeeds when another person can use it for the intended task.

Ideation sketch
A quick drawing for exploring and comparing ideas. Designers and teammates use it to discuss shape, motion, or arrangement before committing to detailed geometry. Label uncertain sizes and assumptions.
CAD model
A digital description of geometry. Designers use it to develop parts, examine how components fit, and support analysis or manufacturing preparation. A realistic appearance alone does not prove that the design works.
Engineering drawing
Selected views with dimensions, tolerances, and notes. People making, assembling, and inspecting the product use this information to understand what is required. See Working Drawings and Title Blocks.

Choose a graphic for brainstorming

Use testing to send the design back for refinement; Practice

Use testing to send the design back for refinement

Begin with the task and its requirements: what must the design do, and what limits must it satisfy? Sketch alternatives, develop promising geometry, then test it against those requirements. Testing may involve calculations, simulation, a prototype, or a combination.

When a test reveals a problem, revise the design and test again. Update the affected graphics so that the model, drawings, and test record describe the same design.

Supporting detail: Addendum 4 — Why the process is a loop.

Choose a graphic for a fit review

Release identifies the information approved for use

Release identifies the information approved for use

Release means approving a defined design state for its intended use through the organization's review process. Before release, check the model, drawing set, and supporting requirements together. A saved file is not automatically an approved file.

A maker needs part requirements; an assembler needs component relationships; an inspector needs criteria for deciding whether the result is acceptable. Match the information to the reader's job. For drawing-based work, use Creating Drawings from CAD Models to prepare the sheets and CAD History, Versions, and Sharing to distinguish an editable design from a preserved milestone.

Supporting detail: Addendum 5 — Does every design require a separate drawing?.

Follow the specified drawing standard and its applicable edition; Practice

Follow the specified drawing standard and its applicable edition

Standards give drawing readers shared rules for interpreting views, lines, dimensions, and symbols. The ASME Y14 series is widely used in US engineering drawing practice; ISO technical drawing standards are widely used internationally. These are not exclusive geographic boundaries. Read the drawing's stated requirements rather than choosing a convention from a country name.

A convention is an accepted way of presenting information. A company may add conventions for sheet layout or numbering, but those choices must remain consistent with the governing requirements. Use the current applicable edition specified for the work; do not silently apply an old classroom example or change an existing drawing's governing edition.

Check units, projection method, and the stated standards before interpreting a drawing. Continue with Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box and Choosing Drawing Views for view interpretation. This overview does not reproduce standard clauses or serve as a compliance checklist.

Check the governing convention

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

First-Angle and Third-Angle Projection

Identify the projection symbol before interpreting where the top and side views sit on the sheet.

Check the projection convention before naming a side view

Check the projection convention before naming a side view

First-angle and third-angle projection can show the same part from the same directions. What changes is where those views are arranged on the sheet.

Look for the projection symbol or an explicit note, often near the title block. Use it with the view labels. If the symbol and the views disagree, resolve the inconsistency before interpreting the part.

View placement relative to the front view
Named viewThird-angleFirst-angle
TopAboveBelow
BottomBelowAbove
Right sideTo the rightTo the left
Left sideTo the leftTo the right

A right-side view is always the view from the part's right. In first-angle projection, it sits to the left of the front view. Do not rename it a left-side view because of its position.

The projection symbol is two views of a shortened cone

The projection symbol is two views of a shortened cone

The trapezoid is the side view of a cone with its tip removed, called a frustum. The two concentric circles are its end view. Their arrangement tells you which projection method is being used.

Supporting detail: Addendum 6 — Use the glass box to explain the swap.

Expect third-angle on U.S. mechanical drawings, then verify it; Practice

Expect third-angle on U.S. mechanical drawings, then verify it

Third-angle is the usual U.S. mechanical drawing convention. A shared convention lets the designer and the person making or inspecting the part interpret the layout the same way. It is a communication choice; neither method changes the part's geometry.

The drawing's declared convention is the deciding information. Country of origin, inch units, or a familiar company name is not a substitute for checking. Drawings cross borders, and CAD templates can use different defaults.

Supporting detail: Addendum 7 — A documented U.S. example, with its scope.

Use the view explorer to switch layouts while holding the part fixed. Then work through the projection self-check.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box

Connect a part's width, height, and depth across aligned views, then unfold the six faces of an imaginary glass box.

Each view looks straight at the part from one direction

Each view looks straight at the part from one direction

A pictorial helps you recognize a part. A multiview drawing helps you describe its shape without the apparent shrinkage of perspective. In orthographic projection, the lines of sight are parallel and perpendicular to the viewing plane.

Choose a front direction and keep the part fixed. Look straight from the front, from above, and from the right. Do not turn the part independently to make each view look convenient.

Front and rear
Show width and height; depth points toward or away from you.
Top and bottom
Show width and depth; height points toward or away from you.
Right and left
Show depth and height; width points toward or away from you.

A face parallel to its viewing plane shows its true shape at the drawing's scale. A face tilted to that plane is foreshortened; a face viewed exactly edge-on becomes a line.

The glass box unfolds into six related views

The glass box unfolds into six related views

Imagine the part inside a transparent box. For third-angle projection, trace what you see onto the box face between you and the part. Each face receives one principal view: front, rear, top, bottom, left, and right.

The names identify the direction you look from. A right-side view means you stood at the part's right, even if a different projection convention puts that view elsewhere on the sheet. Compare First-Angle and Third-Angle Projection.

Predict a view, then compare it with the same block part; Interactive

Predict a view, then compare it with the same block part

Choose a part and a viewing direction in the explorer. Before revealing the view, predict its outline and any step edges. Switch the layout convention and notice what moves on the sheet. The part and the named views stay the same.

These are simple solids with constant depth. Construction guides are teaching aids. The explorer includes the step edges visible or hidden from each selected direction; it is not a dimensioned manufacturing drawing.

Use alignment to follow one feature through the drawing; Checklist

Use alignment to follow one feature through the drawing

  • Identify the front view and confirm the projection convention.
  • Track the same left-to-right position between front and top: they share width.
  • Track the same elevation between front and side: they share height.
  • Compare front-to-back positions between top and side: they share depth.
  • Explain each solid or dashed edge using the shape seen in another view.

At the same scale, a feature cannot be one width in the front view and a different width in the top view. A 45° miter construction can transfer depth between top and side while sketching; that construction line is not an edge of the part.

Supporting detail: Addendum 8 — Why one view can hide an entire change in shape.

Next, decide which views the part actually needs.

Match the pictorial to its front, top, and right views; Practice

Match the pictorial to its front, top, and right views

Identify each numbered candidate using the viewing directions on the pictorial. These candidates are arranged as answer choices, not in a first-angle or third-angle layout.

Use the self-checks to test your choices and read the explanations.

Identify the front Identify the top Identify the right

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Pictorial Sketching

Block out height, width, and depth, then use light construction lines to develop a clear freehand pictorial.

Sketch the idea before committing to CAD

Sketch the idea before committing to CAD

A quick hand sketch lets you compare shapes, explain an idea, and find missing information before building a CAD model. Aim for a readable shape and sensible proportions. A sketch does not need mechanically perfect lines to be useful.

Use a pencil, eraser, and plain or grid paper. Isometric paper can help keep the three directions consistent. Start lightly so you can revise; darken the visible edges only after the overall form works. Add small features last.

Label important features and write any known dimensions. Do not expect someone to recover an exact size by measuring your freehand sketch. For line meanings, see The Alphabet of Lines. CAD sketch tools are covered separately in Sketch Entities and Planes.

Isometric sketches use three equally spaced directions

Isometric sketches use three equally spaced directions

Draw one axis vertically and the other two down to the left and right, each 30° from horizontal. The three outward rays are 120° apart. Edges parallel to these axes keep those directions throughout the sketch; they can extend either way along each axis line.

Use the same scale along all three axis directions. Lay out width, height, and depth along lines parallel to the axes; an isometric grid helps you keep equal intervals consistent.

Supporting detail: Addendum 9 — Isometric drawing and isometric projection use different scales.

For CAD view types, see CAD Model Views and Checks.

Locate sloping edges by endpoints; sketch circles as ellipses

Locate sloping edges by endpoints; sketch circles as ellipses

A non-isometric line is not parallel to any of the three isometric axes. Locate both endpoints using width, depth, and height offsets, then join them. Do not lay the true sloping-edge length directly along its apparent direction on the paper.

For a circle on a face parallel to a principal plane, first sketch its enclosing square as an isometric rhombus. Mark the four side midpoints and sketch a smooth ellipse tangent there. Those are contact points, not sharp corners. Keep the curve inside the rhombus.

The circle-to-ellipse rule here applies to circles on the usual top, front, or side planes of the isometric sketch. Do not draw a round circle on one of these tilted faces.

Build a box, locate the cut, then remove material; Checklist

Build a box, locate the cut, then remove material

Start with the smallest simple box that encloses the part: height, width, depth. In this original example, a corner is removed uniformly through the depth. That makes the front profile a useful starting shape.

  • Compare the overall height, width, and depth before adding detail.
  • Mark where the cut begins and ends on the front profile.
  • Carry those points back along parallel depth lines.
  • Connect matching points to form the new face.
  • Check the remaining edges, then darken visible edges and lighten or erase construction lines.

“Extrude” means carry a profile through a distance. It is a useful mental model only when the cross-section stays constant over that distance. Check other views for features that stop partway through.

Choose isometric for three directions or oblique for a true front face; Practice

Choose isometric for three directions or oblique for a true front face

In an isometric sketch, the three principal directions share one scale, and none of the three principal faces appears in true shape. In an oblique sketch, draw the chosen front face in true shape at the drawing scale, then carry parallel edges back along one receding direction.

A 45° receding direction is common, but it is not required. Full-scale depth is called cavalier; half-scale depth is called cabinet. Keep the chosen depth scale consistent. A circle on the oblique front face stays circular; one on a receding face generally does not.

Both methods use parallel edges rather than perspective vanishing points. Pick the front direction deliberately; see Choosing Drawing Views.

Identify a pictorial Find a non-isometric line Check a circle sketch

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Section Views

Read imaginary cuts, choose a section type, and distinguish cut material from voids and conventional exceptions.

Use an imaginary cut to expose the interior

Use an imaginary cut to expose the interior

A section view shows what is inside a part without making you untangle a group of hidden lines. Imagine cutting the part, removing the material between you and the cutting plane, and looking at what remains.

The cut changes the drawing representation, not the manufactured part. Hatch the material crossed by the plane and show the useful visible edges beyond it. Hidden lines are usually omitted in sections unless needed to make the shape clear.

Start with The Alphabet of Lines and Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box if the line types or viewing directions are unfamiliar. For a sloping face or a small feature, see Auxiliary and Detail Views.

Follow the cutting-plane arrows and match the letters; Checklist

Follow the cutting-plane arrows and match the letters

The cutting-plane line locates the imaginary cut in a parent view. Its arrows point in the direction you look into the remaining part. Matching letters connect that line to a label such as SECTION A–A; the letters do not specify a dimension.

Use a prominent cutting-plane line that extends beyond the part, with thin section lining in the resulting view. Line weight, dash pattern, and arrow size follow the drawing standard and template. These teaching diagrams use blue for cutting planes; color is not required to interpret a drawing.

  • Find both cutting-plane ends and the matching section label.
  • Follow the arrows to decide which side is removed from sight.
  • Trace solid material and voids separately across the plane.
  • Compare the resulting section with the parent view.
Slide a cutting plane and predict the hatch; Interactive

Slide a cutting plane and predict the hatch

Practise reading what a cut exposes. Move plane A–A through a part, decide which regions of SECTION A–A are cut material, then check. Only material the plane passes through is hatched. A hole or slot that the plane crosses stays blank, and so do the surfaces you can see beyond the plane.

Worked example: a full section through the flanged bushing. Plane A–A runs through the axis. Its arrows point toward the back of the part, so the front half is imagined removed and you look at the cut face from the front. Only material the plane passes through is hatched: the bore and counterbore are empty, and the surfaces you see through them lie beyond the plane.

Regions of the bushing section, top to bottom and left to right:

  1. Region 1: Not cut: you see the far wall of the counterbore, about 15.0 mm behind the plane. Draw its edges, but do not hatch it.
  2. Region 2: Cut material: the plane passes through the solid body and flange here, so it is hatched.
  3. Region 3: Not cut: you see the far wall of the through bore, about 10.0 mm behind the plane. Draw its edges, but do not hatch it.
  4. Region 4: Cut material: the plane passes through the solid body and flange here, so it is hatched.

Check the hatched area: each side of the bore contributes wall thickness × height, so 2 × [(20 − 10) × 30 + (30 − 10) × 2 + (30 − 15) × 8] = 920 mm². A hole crossed by the plane removes area from the cut face; it is never hatched.

The three parts are simplified teaching shapes, not dimensioned drawings. Round surfaces are modelled as 96-sided polygons, so every edge lies within 0.03 mm of a true circle at these sizes, and the hatched areas are exact for those polygons. The blind hole has a flat bottom; a drilled hole would end in a cone. Hidden lines are left out, as is usual in sections, and the explorer does not draw tangent edges where a flat face runs smoothly into a curve. It does not apply the rib, spoke and assembly exceptions described in “Hatch cut material, with conventional exceptions” below.

Supporting detail: Addendum 10 — How the explorer decides what is hatched, and its sources.

Full sections cut all the way through the part

Full sections cut all the way through the part

A full section uses one plane through the entire part. For this hollow cylinder, a plane through the axis exposes both walls and the bore. The bore is empty space and receives no hatching.

Half sections combine the exterior and interior

Half sections combine the exterior and interior

A half section is useful for a symmetric part. Imagine removing one quarter with two perpendicular cutting planes. The resulting view shows one half in section and the other half as an exterior view, usually divided by a center line.

It is not a full section with half its hatch erased. The unsectioned half shows the outside, and symmetry supplies the connection between the two halves.

Offset sections reach features that are not in one straight line

Offset sections reach features that are not in one straight line

An offset section jogs the cutting plane to pass through several features. Project the selected parallel portions into one section. The jogs help explain the cut location; they do not create physical edges on the part.

Read the parent view for the holes’ actual locations. Their appearance together in the section does not mean they lie in one straight row.

Broken-out sections expose only a local area

Broken-out sections expose only a local area

A broken-out section removes a limited patch to a chosen depth in an existing view. An irregular break line marks the boundary. Use it to expose a small passage or wall without adding a complete section view.

A separate cutting-plane line is normally unnecessary: the local boundary identifies the area. Depth still matters; a cut that stops before a bore will not reveal it. This differs from a broken view, which merely shortens a long part on the sheet.

Revolved sections show a cross section in place

Revolved sections show a cross section in place

A revolved section turns a cross-sectional slice 90° into the plane of the drawing and places it on the parent view. It is useful for the shape of a bar, spoke, or arm. Show the slice itself, rather than the features behind the cut.

Removed sections place the slice clear of the parent view

Removed sections place the slice clear of the parent view

A removed section places the cross section away from the parent view to keep it readable. Match its identifying letters to the cutting plane. Several removed sections can describe changes along a long part; keep each location unambiguous.

Aligned sections rotate an angled portion into the section plane

Aligned sections rotate an angled portion into the section plane

An aligned section uses intersecting cutting planes through features arranged around an axis. An angled portion is rotated into alignment before it is shown in the section. This makes radial features easier to read.

Do not infer angular spacing from the aligned result. In this disk, one small hole is rotated into the section plane; its original angular position is established by the top view.

Hatch cut material, with conventional exceptions

Hatch cut material, with conventional exceptions

Use thin, evenly spaced diagonal lines, commonly near 45° to the main outline. Change the angle when the hatch would be confused with an edge. Keep a part’s hatch consistent; distinguish adjacent assembly parts by changing hatch angle or spacing.

  • Voids: holes and open spaces are never hatched as solid material.
  • Ribs, webs, and spokes: a cut along their length generally leaves them unhatched so they do not look like a thick solid wall. A transverse cut through their thickness is hatched.
  • Shafts and fasteners in assembly sections: when cut lengthwise through their axes, solid shafts, bolts, nuts, washers, pins, and similar standard parts are commonly shown unsectioned. A transverse shaft section can be hatched; “never hatch a shaft” is too broad.

An unhatched region may be empty space, an uncut surface, or a conventionally unsectioned component. Use its outline and the other views to decide which.

Supporting detail: Addendum 11 — Drawing standards and scope.

Create the section from a CAD drawing view, then inspect it; Checklist; Practice

Create the section from a CAD drawing view, then inspect it

Start with a model-based parent drawing view. Choose a section command, define the cut, set its viewing direction, and place the result. These drawing operations do not remove material from the design model.

Full, half, and offset
Use a section-view command with a straight, half-section, or jogged cutting path. SOLIDWORKS calls the main tool Section View; Onshape uses Section view. Available half-section controls differ by application.
Aligned
Choose the aligned section option and define the intersection and angled portions. SOLIDWORKS uses its Section View PropertyManager; Onshape names the tool Aligned section view.
Broken-out
Define a closed local profile and a cut depth. The tools are Broken-out Section in SOLIDWORKS and Broken-out section view in Onshape.
Removed and revolved
Create a slice-only section, then place it apart or rotate and position it in the parent view. SOLIDWORKS documents Removed Section and a rotated-section workflow combining a break with section views. Onshape’s Show cut geometry only option can produce a slice without background geometry; check placement and rotation support in the installed version rather than assuming a dedicated revolved-section button.
  • Check that the plane crosses the intended features and the arrows face the intended direction.
  • Check the label, view scale, hidden-edge visibility, and hatch regions.
  • Exclude applicable assembly components from the cut and inspect ribs separately.
  • After a model change, update the drawing and recheck cut references and annotations.

Supporting detail: Addendum 12 — Vendor help for the drawing tools.

Practice identifying a section Practice hatch conventions

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

The Alphabet of Lines

Read line patterns, weights, and endpoints to distinguish part edges from centers, dimensions, cuts, and alternate positions.

Read the pattern before deciding what the line means

Read the pattern before deciding what the line means

Every line on an engineering drawing has a job. Some describe the part; others tell you how to measure it, where to look, or how a view was made. Treating every line as a physical edge gives you the wrong part.

Use three clues together: pattern (solid or dashed), weight (thick or thin), and context (arrows, letters, numbers, and nearby features). A thin solid line alone could be a dimension, an extension, a leader, or section hatching.

Visible and hidden lines describe edges; center lines locate axes

Visible and hidden lines describe edges; center lines locate axes

Visible / object
A relatively thick, continuous line shows an edge or outline you can see from this viewing direction.
Hidden
A thin series of short, evenly spaced dashes shows an edge concealed by material. A hole may appear as a visible circle in one view and two hidden lines in another.
Center
A thin long-short pattern locates a center, axis, or symmetry reference. The center line through a cylinder is not a seam in the cylinder.
Phantom
A thin long-short-short pattern can show an alternate position, repeated detail, or a nearby part used as a reference. An open position of a lever does not mean there are two levers.

Read all views together. A line's visibility depends on where you are looking from. The same edge can be solid in one view and dashed in another.

Arrows, notes, and hatching tell you what to do with a view

Arrows, notes, and hatching tell you what to do with a view

Dimension
A thin line with arrowheads identifies the extent of a measurement. Read the associated value; do not measure the picture on your screen.
Extension
A thin line carries a feature's location out to a dimension line. A small gap usually separates it from the part outline.
Leader
A thin line connects a note to the feature it describes, usually with an arrow at an edge or a dot on a surface. Follow it to its endpoint.
Cutting plane
A prominent line marks an imaginary cut used to expose the interior. Read its arrows for the viewing direction and its letters to find the matching section, such as A–A. The line pattern can vary; arrows and identification matter.
Section / hatch
Thin parallel strokes inside a section view identify material crossed by the imaginary cut. They are not grooves machined into the part.
Break
A short freehand break or a long thin line with zigzags marks an omitted portion of a view. The actual part is not necessarily broken; a long uniform member can be shortened on paper while its dimension gives the full length.

For units and decimals, use Measurement Language. For allowable variation, use Tolerances and Fits. Creating the dimension callouts comes next in Drawing Dimensioning.

When lines coincide, do not invent a second feature; Practice

When lines coincide, do not invent a second feature

Where a visible edge and a hidden edge project to exactly the same place, read the visible line. Where a hidden edge and a center line coincide, read the hidden line; the center line may still be identifiable where it extends beyond the edge.

A crossing is different from an overlap. Two lines crossing on the sheet do not prove that two physical edges meet in space. Check another view before deciding.

Supporting detail: Addendum 13 — Why context matters more than one dash.

Practice identifying lines

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Visualizing Parts from Multiview Drawings

Track the same surfaces through front, top, and side views, then reconstruct a pictorial without guessing hidden geometry.

Rebuild a part by combining shared dimensions; Checklist

Rebuild a part by combining shared dimensions

A multiview drawing gives several descriptions of one fixed part. Read them together: front and top share width, front and side share height, and top and side share depth. Review Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box and confirm the projection convention before interpreting positions on the sheet.

  • Identify the front direction and the overall width, height, and depth.
  • Sketch a light enclosing box using isometric construction.
  • Choose a recognizable profile and locate its corners in the box.
  • Use the other views to decide which features continue, stop, or change along the depth.
  • Account for every visible and hidden edge before darkening the pictorial.

Do not assume that a front profile extends all the way through. The top or side view must support that interpretation. If two shapes still fit the information, identify the missing view or dimension rather than inventing a feature.

Match a surface by its boundaries, not its apparent shape

Match a surface by its boundaries, not its apparent shape

Face A in this original example is the front face. Face B is the sloping face made by removing a corner through the full depth. Follow their corner positions and shared boundaries across the views.

A appears in true shape in the front view. From above, all its points have the same front-to-back position, so it collapses to the front boundary line. From the right, it also appears edge-on. B appears as a sloping edge in front, but as a foreshortened area in top and right.

Supporting detail: Addendum 14 — One drawn line can represent several boundaries.

Normal, inclined, and oblique describe a flat surface relative to the view planes

Normal, inclined, and oblique describe a flat surface relative to the view planes

Normal surface
Parallel to one principal projection plane and perpendicular to the other two. It shows true shape in one principal view and an edge in the other two. Face A is an example.
Inclined surface
Perpendicular to one principal plane and tilted to the other two. It shows an edge in one principal view and a foreshortened area in the other two. Face B is an example.
Oblique surface
Tilted to all three principal planes, with none parallel or perpendicular to it. It shows a foreshortened area in all three principal views; none shows true shape or an edge view.

Here “oblique surface” describes a face orientation. “Oblique sketch” describes a pictorial drawing method. A part with an inclined face can be drawn with either isometric or oblique sketching.

Turn a pictorial back into views one direction at a time; Practice

Turn a pictorial back into views one direction at a time

Keep the front direction fixed. For the front view, discard depth and plot width against height. For the top, discard height and plot width against depth. For the side, discard width and plot depth against height. Include changes of surface inside the outside outline.

Before checking, explain which boundary remains visible from above and where it lies relative to the width. A matching outside rectangle alone is not enough.

Match the top view Find an edge view Classify a surface Recognize an oblique surface

Predict and reveal views in the projection explorer; Interactive; Practice

Predict and reveal views in the projection explorer

Choose a part, predict the missing view on paper, then reveal it. Change the part and repeat. Use the alignment guides to check shared dimensions. Changing the sheet layout changes view placement, not the part.

On paper: cover the top view, predict its outer rectangle and the line where the sloping face meets the flat top, then uncover it.

The explorer uses simple stepped solids of constant depth. Use the separate static example above to study the sloping surface.

Check a reconstruction assumption

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings

Working Drawings and Title Blocks

Distinguish part and assembly drawings, then use title blocks and revision records to identify the information that applies.

Send the drawing type that answers the reader's job; Practice

Send the drawing type that answers the reader's job

Detail or part drawing
Defines an individual part for making and inspection, using the necessary views, dimensions, tolerances, material information, and notes. A part drawing is not the same thing as an enlarged detail view.
Assembly drawing
Shows how components relate and fit together. It may include item identification, assembly requirements, and overall or interface dimensions. See Exploded Views and Bills of Materials for exploded views, item balloons, and parts lists.
Working-drawing set
The coordinated drawings needed to make and assemble a product: typically assembly drawings and the required part drawings, with supporting lists and notes as needed. A set may span several sheets and drawing numbers.

An assembly view alone usually does not provide every requirement needed to manufacture each component. Confirm that the recipient has the required sheets and revisions.

Choose a drawing for making a part Choose a drawing for assembly

Read identity, units, and scale before reading dimensions; Practice

Read identity, units, and scale before reading dimensions

The title block identifies the drawing and records key information about it. Its layout varies. Read field labels; do not assume a familiar-looking border has familiar settings.

The part name tells you what the item is; the part or drawing number identifies the controlled record. Those numbers may be different. Units tell you how to interpret dimension values. Scale describes the displayed view size relative to the object, not the part's actual size. Check individual view labels for scale overrides, and use stated dimensions rather than measuring a print.

Find the units Interpret sheet scale

Find material, tolerances, and responsibility in the block or notes; Practice

Find material, tolerances, and responsibility in the block or notes

General practice includes fields or notes for material, general tolerances, revision, and drawn/checked information. Some templates also carry dates, approval status, finish requirements, or a projection symbol. A material field may refer to a separate specification; read that reference rather than guessing from the appearance of the model.

A tolerance states the permitted variation from a requirement. Read the scope of the general tolerance note and any specific tolerances at features. Displaying more decimal places is not, by itself, a complete tolerance instruction. See Dimension Anatomy and Placement, Choosing Dimensions, and Hole and Feature Callouts.

Drawn and checked entries record responsibility. They do not replace the organization's approval or release process. Missing or conflicting requirements need clarification before the drawing is used.

Locate a material requirement

Match the revision record to the drawing being used; Checklist; Practice

Match the revision record to the drawing being used

The title block commonly shows the drawing's current revision identifier. A revision block or associated change record explains changes, often with a description, date, and authorization. Exact fields and identifier sequences depend on the organization's system.

A new file date alone does not prove that a drawing is the authorized revision. Match its number and revision to the release record for the job. Related parts may legitimately have different revision identifiers; they must be the approved combination.

  • Match the drawing and part identifiers to the item you need.
  • Confirm the required revision and approval status.
  • Confirm that every referenced sheet, note, and parts list is available.
  • Read change descriptions and inspect affected views and requirements.

Check a revision

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Dimensioning

Choosing Dimensions

Break a part into simple forms, define each feature’s size and location, and remove redundant requirements.

Ask what information is necessary to make this part

Ask what information is necessary to make this part

Start with the geometry, not with the dimension tool. Break the part into familiar forms: blocks, cylinders, holes, steps, slots and arcs.

Size dimensions
Describe the feature itself: a block’s length, width and thickness; a hole’s diameter; a slot’s width and length.
Location dimensions
Place that feature relative to other features or a chosen origin. A hole diameter alone does not say where the hole goes.

Locate a round hole by its center, not by a tangent edge that moves when the diameter changes. Choose reference surfaces that make sense for how the part fits and is checked. A formal datum has a specific meaning in geometric tolerancing; an arbitrary sketch origin is not automatically a datum.

Dimension a feature in the view that shows its shape

Dimension a feature in the view that shows its shape

Contour dimensioning keeps a feature’s dimensions with the view where its outline is clearest. Put a hole size on a view showing its circle. Put a step’s height where the step is visible. Use a section or another suitable view for an internal feature.

For the beginner drawings here, do not dimension to hidden lines: choose a view that exposes the feature. Keep the dimensions of one feature together when practical. See the Reading Drawings group in Engineering Graphics for projection, section views and view selection.

Build the dimension scheme in a deliberate order; Checklist

Build the dimension scheme in a deliberate order

  • Identify the simple forms and list the features that need size, location or orientation information.
  • Choose the views that show those features clearly. Establish useful reference edges or surfaces.
  • Add the main body sizes. Leave space for smaller feature dimensions nearer the outline.
  • Add feature sizes and end conditions, such as a hole diameter and THRU.
  • Locate the feature centers, steps and other boundaries from the chosen references.
  • Check completeness, remove duplicate requirements, and arrange the lines for readability.

Do not add dimensions just because the CAD system offers them. Review each imported model dimension for purpose, view, placement and duplication.

Give each independent requirement once

Give each independent requirement once

Completeness means every feature is defined. It does not mean every possible distance is dimensioned. A feature may need several dimensions, but the same size or location requirement should not be repeated in another view or restated by a closed chain.

A closed chain gives all the segments and their total as controlling dimensions. Remove one link, or make a useful derived value a reference dimension. Which link to remove depends on what the part must do.

Supporting detail: Addendum 15 — Why nominal arithmetic is not enough.

Parentheses mark information, not an extra acceptance requirement; Practice

Parentheses mark information, not an extra acceptance requirement

A reference dimension is shown in parentheses, such as (1.50). It helps the reader without imposing another manufacturing or inspection requirement. Use one when the derived value is useful; leave it out when it only adds clutter.

In the two-hole example, .80 and 2.30 can control the centers while (1.50) reports their nominal spacing. Parentheses do not mean that the physical distance cannot vary.

A basic dimension, shown in a rectangular box, is different: it supplies a theoretically exact value for a geometric tolerance scheme. It does not demand a physically perfect part. See Tolerances and Fits before interpreting limits or fits.

Find a redundant dimension Count the required dimensions

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Dimensioning

Dimension Anatomy and Placement

Read the lines, arrows and text of a dimension, then arrange them so the part stays easy to understand.

A dimension connects a number to a specific feature

A dimension connects a number to a specific feature

A drawing shows the shape. Its dimensions tell the reader how big the features are and where they belong. Read the stated value; do not measure the picture.

Dimension line
Runs in the direction being measured. Its arrowheads mark the extent of the dimension.
Extension line
Projects an edge, center or other point out to the dimension. Leave a visible gap at the part and continue a little beyond the last related dimension line.
Arrowheads and text
The arrows identify the endpoints; the text gives the value and any needed symbol. Use a consistent arrow style and readable text size.
Leader
A thin line connecting a note or callout to its feature. A hole leader ends with an arrow on the circle, directed toward its center.

Keep the dimension line separate from the part outline. A visible edge or centerline is not a substitute for a dimension line. For line types and views, see the Engineering Graphics collection’s Reading Drawings group.

Put dimensions outside the view, with the shortest nearest the part

Put dimensions outside the view, with the shortest nearest the part

Keep the outline clear. Put short dimensions close to the view and longer dimensions farther out. This also reduces the number of extension lines that cross dimension lines.

A dimension inside the view can be appropriate when it is clearer there or avoids an excessively long leader. The aim is clarity, not an empty interior at any cost.

Leave room for the lines, arrows and text

Leave room for the lines, arrows and text

Use at least 10 mm from the part outline to the first dimension line and 6 mm between successive parallel dimension lines as layout guides. Those are distances on the drawing sheet, regardless of the part’s scale. The familiar inch drafting guides are about 3/8 in and 1/4 in; they are rounded guides, not exact conversions.

Keep the gap at the part visible and extend the extension line slightly beyond the dimension line. About 2 mm of overrun is a useful drafting target. Increase spacing when the annotation needs more room.

Supporting detail: Addendum 16 — Which parts are standards, and which are layout guides?.

Keep text readable from the bottom of the sheet

Keep text readable from the bottom of the sheet

Use unidirectional text for the ordinary linear dimensions here: the numbers read from the bottom even when the dimension line is vertical. Leave clear space around the number. On a horizontal line, the text may sit above it or in a break in it.

Stagger values on several parallel dimension lines so they are easier to separate. Keep lettering free of part outlines, extension lines and leaders.

Supporting detail: Addendum 17 — Why older drawings may look different.

Rearrange crossing lines before accepting clutter; Practice

Rearrange crossing lines before accepting clutter

Move dimensions or notes to avoid crossing dimension lines, extension lines and leaders wherever practical. Keep a leader short, with a clear arrow target and a short horizontal landing next to the note.

If extension lines must cross, normally leave them continuous. Do not introduce gaps that make their endpoints ambiguous. A break near an arrowhead can preserve its readability.

Next: choose the information the drawing needs. Practice placement

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Dimensioning

Hole and Feature Callouts

Read radii, diameters, slots, repeated features and hole notes, including the units and decimal places on an inch drawing.

Read the units before reading the numbers

Read the units before reading the numbers

Find the drawing’s unit note or title block first. On an inch drawing, .625 means 0.625 inch, not 625 inches and not millimeters. The unit need not be repeated beside every value when the drawing states it.

Decimal-inch dimensions conventionally omit the leading zero below one inch. Keep trailing zeros: .50 and .500 have the same nominal size, but may select different rows in the drawing’s general tolerance block. There is no universal “three decimals means ±.005” rule; read the actual block and any local tolerance.

An angle still needs its angle notation: 90°. Mixed units must be identified. For units and precision, use Measurement Language; for tolerance values, limits and fits, use Tolerances and Fits.

Use a diameter for a full circle and a radius for an arc

Use a diameter for a full circle and a radius for an arc

⌀ before a value means diameter. R before a value means radius. Thus ⌀.60 describes a full circular diameter of .60, while R.30 describes an arc radius of .30. The values are related, but the callouts describe different kinds of feature.

n X means the requirement applies in n places. A repeated size still needs an unambiguous pattern: center coordinates, spacing, or a fully defined bolt circle. A sketch that merely looks evenly spaced is not enough.

A round-ended slot needs size, location and direction

A round-ended slot needs size, location and direction

For a straight slot with semicircular ends, give its width and either its overall length or the distance between the end centers. Make the chosen meaning clear. Then locate the slot and establish its direction relative to the part.

Do not control the width, end radius, center spacing and overall length all at once. That repeats the relationships already built into the semicircular-ended shape. If a slot is not semicircular-ended, this shortcut does not apply.

Read a hole callout from the main hole to the added recess

Read a hole callout from the main hole to the added recess

The first size usually describes the main hole. Read the remaining symbols with the values immediately following them. All examples below are invented decimal-inch teaching values.

CalloutHow it reads
⌀.30 THRUA .30 diameter opening goes through the part. THRU is an end condition, not a numeric depth.
⌀.30 ↧ .55A .30 diameter blind hole has .55 depth to the full-diameter portion. A drill-point cone, if present, extends farther unless otherwise specified.
⌀.30 THRU
⌴ ⌀.60 ↧ .15		The .30 through hole has a cylindrical, flat-bottomed counterbore: .60 diameter and .15 deep from the entry surface.
⌀.30 THRU
⌵ ⌀.60 × 90°		The .30 through hole has a conical countersink: .60 major diameter at the entry and a 90° included angle, measured across both sides of the cone.

Read the leader and section view to identify the entry side. A hole callout supplies size and end condition; it still needs location dimensions. A countersink angle is not automatically 90°.

A spotface provides a local flat seat

A spotface provides a local flat seat

A spotface provides a flat circular seating surface around a hole. Its modern symbol puts SF inside the counterbore-shaped mark. Older drawings may use the counterbore mark with a note or context identifying the spotface.

A spotface may have a stated depth or remaining material thickness. If neither is specified, the ASME convention is the minimum depth needed to clean up the specified diameter. Do not invent a depth from the sketch.

Supporting detail: Addendum 18 — Reading old and new symbol styles.

Change a hole and watch its callout change; Interactive; Practice

Change a hole and watch its callout change

Predict which line will change before changing a control. Compare counterbore depth with countersink angle, then change the main diameter while keeping the recess diameter fixed.

Static example: 2X ⌀.300 THRU / ⌴ ⌀.600 ↧ .150 means two holes, each .300 diameter through, each with a .600 diameter counterbore .150 deep. Their positions must be defined elsewhere.

The section sketches above provide a printable comparison of the same hole types. The live builder uses invented dimensions and an ideal section; it does not select a fastener, tolerance or manufacturing process.

Read a counterbore Check a slot length

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

CAD Certification Preparation

Build dependable modeling habits, check your work, and use official sources to plan an entry-level CAD certification attempt.

Use certification as a goal for building dependable CAD skills

Use certification as a goal for building dependable CAD skills

A CAD certification gives you a way to demonstrate skills assessed by its provider. Preparing for one can help you become more productive, build models that survive changes, and describe your skills on a resume. Passing does not guarantee a job or prove that every design you make will work.

The Certified SOLIDWORKS Associate (CSWA) is the worked case here, offered through Dassault Systèmes' SOLIDWORKS certification program. Its hands-on modeling workflow does not describe every vendor exam: some routes use selected-response questions, testing-center delivery, platform roles, or different software-access rules. Compare those routes first in CAD Certifications. CourseWiki is an independent learning resource and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Dassault Systèmes.

Find the current exam rules before you register; Checklist

Find the current exam rules before you register

Start at the official SOLIDWORKS certification program, then select the CSWA Design Associate page. Check the exact credential name: similarly named certifications can assess different tools.

  • Read the current exam description, skill coverage, format, length, question count, passing rules, and any section weights on the official page.
  • Follow the official registration or purchase route; confirm the current price and any voucher conditions before paying.
  • Check software, computer, account, and testing-client requirements, plus the rules for permitted resources and retakes.
  • Find the official sample or practice resources linked from the certification page and read their use instructions.

For current numerical exam details, see the official page. This guide does not reproduce an exam specification, exam questions, answer keys, or sample parts. The official certification FAQ is another starting point for registration and testing questions. Academic and ordinary CSWP routes have different conditions, and student software access does not by itself prove an exam voucher is included.

Practise reading, modeling, assembling, and checking

Practise reading, modeling, assembling, and checking

Use these general skill areas to organize practice; use the official description to confirm what your chosen certification assesses.

  • Read a drawing: identify views, dimensions, and feature notes before building. Start with Drawing Terminology Review.
  • Sketch deliberately: use dimensions and geometric relations to control size and shape. Review Geometric Relations in Sketches.
  • Build and revise parts: choose features that express the shape, then change a dimension and check the result. Review Feature-based Modeling.
  • Assemble components: place parts and constrain their intended positions or motion with mates. Review Assembly Files and Mates.
  • Inspect the result: measure dimensions, check mass properties, and confirm the correct model state. Review CAD Model Views and Checks.
Check geometry, units, and material before trusting mass; Checklist; Practice

Check geometry, units, and material before trusting mass

For a uniform solid, mass = density × volume. Use compatible units: density in g/cm³ multiplied by volume in cm³ gives mass in g. To convert mm³ to cm³, divide by 1,000 because 1 cm³ = 10 × 10 × 10 mm³.

Changing only the displayed units changes the number and unit label, not the physical size or mass. Entering a dimension in the wrong units changes the geometry. Choosing a different density changes mass even when the shape stays the same.

  • Confirm the drawing's units and the units used when entering dimensions.
  • Check overall dimensions, holes, and removed material against all relevant views.
  • Assign the specified material or density to the intended bodies or components.
  • Rebuild after edits; confirm the intended configuration and which bodies or components are included.
  • Read the requested quantity and its output units before recording an answer.

Supporting detail: Addendum 19 — Why matching mass does not prove the shape is right.

Practise mass from volume Practise cubic units Check a unit change

Build accuracy first, then practise with a time limit

Build accuracy first, then practise with a time limit

Choose an original, ungraded drawing you have permission to use. Build the part without following a click-by-click demonstration. Explain how each view supports the geometry, then check the dimensions and material. Repeat with a changed dimension to see whether the model updates as intended.

Once that process is reliable, set a practice time limit. Include time to read, model, check, and save. Record where you lose time and practise that skill next. During an actual attempt, follow the provider's rules about navigation, returning to questions, and saving work.

Keep a short error log: drawing interpretation, sketch control, feature choice, assembly position, units, or material. Rebuild after correcting the cause instead of memorizing the previous answer.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

CAD Certifications

Compare current mechanical CAD certification paths, distinguish requirements from recommendations, and verify the route before registering.

Use a certification to document assessed skills, not to replace design experience

Use a certification to document assessed skills, not to replace design experience

A CAD certification is a provider's record that you passed a defined assessment. Depending on the program, that assessment may cover drawing interpretation, sketches, parts, assemblies, documentation, collaboration, manufacturing, or analysis. It can give a learner a concrete practice goal and give an employer one more piece of evidence about a specific product or workflow.

Its meaning is bounded. A credential does not guarantee employment, prove that every model is manufacturable, or replace a portfolio, coursework, supervised practice, and engineering judgment. Product names and versions also matter: proficiency in one CAD system does not automatically transfer to every other system.

This overview leads with mechanical CAD. Architecture and construction, CAM, simulation, additive manufacturing, product-data management, and platform roles are useful branches when they match the work you want to do. Program information below was checked against official sources on October 29, 2026; recheck the linked catalog before registering.

Choose the product and work first, then the credential level

Choose the product and work first, then the credential level

Do not begin by looking for a universal Associate → Professional → Expert ladder. Providers use those words differently, and some products offer only selected levels. Begin with the software and tasks used in your course, internship, workplace, or intended field.

Core mechanical design
Look for sketching, parametric part modeling, assemblies, drawings, dimensions, materials, and model checks.
Specialized design
Sheet metal, surfacing, weldments, mold tools, drawing tools, and generative design usually require narrower practice than a general design credential.
Manufacturing and additive
CAM, turning, milling, additive-process, and design-for-manufacturing credentials connect geometry to process planning. They are not substitutes for machine or shop authorization.
Simulation
Static, thermal, flow, frequency, nonlinear, and other analysis credentials assess both software operation and interpretation. Passing does not make an unchecked result physically valid.
Platform and data roles
Cloud collaboration, revisions, lifecycle, PDM, and administrator credentials may assess data workflows rather than only geometry creation.

Read the assessed skills on the exact credential page. A badge for completing a course, a training certificate, and a certification earned by passing an assessment are not automatically the same thing.

Compare SOLIDWORKS and Autodesk mechanical paths

Compare SOLIDWORKS and Autodesk mechanical paths

SOLIDWORKS

The official SOLIDWORKS catalog groups the general design path as Design Associate, Design Professional, and Design Expert, but the levels assess different depth rather than the same checklist three times.

Design Associate (CSWA)
Foundational sketches, common part features, patterns, dimensions, materials and mass properties, component insertion and mates, drawing views, and annotations.
Design Professional (CSWP)
Professional parametric part design from drawings, linked dimensions and equations, configurations and design tables, mass-property changes, and assembly modeling across three segments.
Design Expert (CSWE)
Advanced part and assembly problem solving, including multibody/imported geometry, complex features, in-context work, configurations, and advanced bills of materials. Eligibility requires CSWP plus at least four of exactly these five advanced-topic exams: Sheet Metal, Weldments, Surfacing, Mold Tools/Mold Making, and Drawing Tools.

Those five design specialties form the CSWE prerequisite set. Other Professional credentials—such as CAM, MBD, API, and Flow Simulation—assess valuable but different work and are not listed as substitutes in the CSWE requirement. Additive Manufacturing Associate assesses processes, materials, design, slicing, and preparation without requiring SOLIDWORKS software during the assessment.

The simulation family is separate: Simulation Associate covers statics, materials, loads, mesh, and result checks; Simulation Professional adds static, frequency, thermal, beam/shell, and convergence work; Simulation Expert requires CSWP, CSWA-S, and CSWP-S and adds advanced contact, composites, thermal, dynamics, and nonlinear analysis. Flow Simulation Professional is another specialty, not a step in that three-credential prerequisite chain.

Cloud xDesign and xShape credentials are not alternate names for desktop CSWA/CSWP. The xDesign Professional and xShape Professional pages require the relevant app, prescribed training, 3DSwymer Associate, ENOVIA Collaborative Industry Innovator Associate, and a new collaboration space. Exact student-cloud bundle mapping remains unclear, so confirm access before choosing one.

Route matters for students. Through the Academic Certification program, free exams depend on the school being an Academic Certification Provider, an active subscription, and region-specific license minimums; this is not an entitlement for every student. The current Design Premium for Students offer separately lists CSWA and CSWP attempts, while free Design Standard software does not list them. Recheck the current offer before purchase. Ordinary CSWP publishes no general prior-certification requirement, except that K–12 students using an Academic Certification Provider must first pass CSWA. The distinct CSWP-Academic route requires CSWA-Academic at least 30 days earlier and qualified, proctored institutional delivery.

Autodesk

Autodesk names four broad levels: Certified User (ACU), Certified Associate (ACA), Certified Professional (ACP), and Certified Expert (ACE). Not every product has every level, and the official overview does not establish a universal prerequisite ladder.

Mechanical starting points include ACU exams for AutoCAD, Inventor, and Fusion; ACA in CAD for Mechanical Design; ACP in Inventor for Mechanical Design, AutoCAD for Design and Drafting, and Design for Manufacturing; and ACE in Generative Design for Manufacturing. Optional extensions include Fusion CAM credentials, ACP in Simulation for Static Stress Analysis, and AEC credentials for Revit, Civil 3D, and BIM management.

ACU registration runs through Certiport; Autodesk's current ACU guidance says exams may be delivered online or in person, so do not assume a testing-center-only route. ACA, ACP, and ACE pages instead route candidates through Autodesk's application/dashboard to Pearson VUE or OnVUE. Those ACA/ACP/ACE exams use selected-response questions rather than live CAD software, so preparation should include concepts and workflow decisions as well as software practice. See Autodesk certification support for current policies and preparation routes. Free Autodesk education software and free learning resources do not establish a free exam or student discount.

Compare Onshape, Creo, NX, and Solid Edge

Compare Onshape, Creo, NX, and Solid Edge

Onshape
The live Learning Center certification catalog lists Certified Onshape Associate for parts, multipart design, assemblies, drawings, and collaboration, and Certified Onshape Professional for advanced modeling, motion, in-context work, versioning, branching, and linked-data collaboration. No Associate prerequisite is published for Professional. Register through the Learning Center and its Training Dashboard. A student Associate voucher has been described only through a conditional preparation route; current course access and voucher availability must be confirmed.
PTC Creo
The current PTC Learning Connector uses Product Proficiency for foundational sketches, features, assemblies, properties, and analysis; Modeling Specialist for advanced design intent, sketches, and solids; and Surfacing, Sheetmetal, Assembly, and Documentation specialists for their named workflows. Older User/Associate/Professional labels should not replace the live catalog. Enroll through the specific Learning Connector exam with appropriate active LEARN access; learning paths are recommended, and the current FAQ says prior certifications are not prerequisites. A separate academic certification-only route offers Product Proficiency, Modeling Specialist, Assembly Specialist, and Documentation Specialist after Proxi.id academic verification. It does not include every specialist or prove a universal student entitlement.
Siemens NX
The live Siemens Xcelerator Academy catalog lists NX Design Associate for solid and assembly models, modeling strategies, parametric/non-parametric methods, and interpart links; NX Design Professional adds curves and surfaces, PMI, validation, downstream model use, and drafting. The NX Design learning map makes Associate a prerequisite for Professional. Register from the catalog's Buy route. Optional NX CAM Associate/Professional and Additive Manufacturing Associate paths assess manufacturing work. Academic discounts or free vouchers may depend on institutional licensing; no universal student entitlement is established.
Siemens Solid Edge
The Solid Edge registry publishes Associate, Professional, and Expert. Associate covers introductory parts, assemblies, sketches, and drawings; Professional adds advanced synchronous, sheet-metal, assembly, and documentation work. Associate before Professional is recommended, not stated as mandatory; Expert requires Professional and assesses advanced ordered/synchronous modeling and detailing. Use Getting Started to register, complete the profile, review the guide, and select an exam. Enrollment pages currently display the exams as free, but verify region and delivered software version.
Keep CATIA V5 and 3DEXPERIENCE credentials separate

Keep CATIA V5 and 3DEXPERIENCE credentials separate

Dassault Systèmes publishes two different families. 3DEXPERIENCE role certifications include Associate roles such as Mechanical Designer, Mechanical & Shape Designer, SheetMetal Designer, and Function Driven Generative Designer. Associate exams use the Edu Space and certification-credit route with access to the appropriate roles/apps. The Professional registry covers advanced Mechanical Designer, Function Driven Generative Designer, and SheetMetal Designer work through authorized certification centers—public centers for general candidates or private academic centers for their students. Role trigrams identify software roles, not separate marketed exam codes.

CATIA V5 certification is another center-delivered family, marketed at Associate and Expert levels for Part Design, Assembly Design, and Surface Design. Its catalog describes training and regular practice as preparation, but the inspected pages do not publish a prior Associate credential as a universal Expert gate. Contact an authorized center for the available V5 route rather than registering through the 3DEXPERIENCE Associate Edu Space.

Student CATIA/3DEXPERIENCE offers can bundle software and exams under eligibility, billing-country, age, and noncommercial-use conditions. Official pages conflict on the exact bundled exam roster and renewal wording, so confirm the cart and current student terms rather than promising a particular set of credentials.

Separate prerequisites, preparation, access, and payment; Checklist

Separate prerequisites, preparation, access, and payment

  • Credential prerequisite: a prior certification the exact exam page says you must hold. Examples include the published CSWE, SOLIDWORKS Simulation Expert, NX Design Professional, and Solid Edge Expert chains.
  • Recommended preparation: experience hours, courses, learning paths, or practice described as readiness guidance. Do not silently convert a recommendation into an admission rule.
