  • Software or platform access: the app, version, role, testing client, collaboration space, or live software needed to prepare for or take that route.
  • Registration condition: account, identity, age/consent, testing-center, remote-proctor, institutional, region, or academic-verification requirements.
  • Payment condition: a public purchase, institutional voucher, subscription benefit, bundle, or conditional student offer. Free student software is not the same as a free exam.

Voucher expiration and credential validity are also different. For example, Certiport governs ACU credential policy while Autodesk's other credentials use Autodesk/Pearson routes. Confirm the exact program, country, tax, proctoring, retake, voucher, and validity terms immediately before paying or scheduling.

Use one verified route from comparison through preparation

Use one verified route from comparison through preparation

  1. Name the product and work you want to demonstrate: general mechanical design, drawings, manufacturing, simulation, or data workflow.
  2. Open the provider's current catalog and the exact credential page. Record the title, assessed skills, delivery route, and published prerequisites.
  3. Mark recommendations separately from requirements. Confirm that you can access the needed software, account, testing center, or remote-proctor setup.
  4. Ask your institution about participation or vouchers without assuming it has them. Verify any student offer, region, expiration, and checkout total directly.
  5. Use official preparation materials without copying exam questions, answer keys, or protected sample parts. Practise the underlying workflow with original drawings and models.

For a worked preparation case, continue to CAD Certification Preparation. It uses CSWA to organize drawing, modeling, assembly, units, material, mass-property, checking, and revision practice while keeping the official exam specification outside CourseWiki.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

CAD Files and Documents

Choose the right container for parts, assemblies, and drawings, then check templates, units, and references.

Choose a part, assembly, or drawing for the work you need to do

Choose a part, assembly, or drawing for the work you need to do

A part describes geometry. An assembly positions components relative to one another. A drawing communicates that design through views, dimensions, and notes. Start by deciding which job you need the document to do.

SOLIDWORKS part: .sldprt
Contains part geometry and its modeling features. A part can contain one body or multiple bodies; the file extension does not mean there is exactly one solid.
SOLIDWORKS assembly: .sldasm
References components, including parts and subassemblies, and stores their arrangement and assembly relationships.
SOLIDWORKS drawing: .slddrw
Usually references a part or assembly to generate drawing views. It is a separate document from the model.

Continue with Feature-based Modeling, Assembly Files and Mates, or Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box for the modeling and drawing methods.

An Onshape document holds tabs inside a workspace

An Onshape document holds tabs inside a workspace

An Onshape document is a container for related design information. Open a workspace to edit that information, then select the tab for the task.

  • Part Studio: create geometry using sketches and features. One Part Studio can produce several related parts.
  • Assembly: insert and position part or subassembly instances and define their relationships.
  • Drawing: create drawing sheets and views of models.
  • Tabs and tab folders: organize the document's contents. Use the Tab Manager to find a tab when the row becomes crowded. A tab folder organizes tabs; it does not mate parts together.

Several parts created together in a Part Studio are not automatically an assembly with motion relationships. See Sketch Entities and Planes to begin geometry and CAD History, Versions, and Sharing to distinguish a workspace from a version.

Supporting detail: Addendum 20 — Vendor help for the document model.

Check the template and units before entering dimensions; Checklist

Check the template and units before entering dimensions

A template supplies starting settings. In SOLIDWORKS, part, assembly, and drawing templates use .prtdot, .asmdot, and .drwdot. Choose the appropriate template, then verify the new document's units. A familiar template name is not proof that its settings are right.

In Onshape, check workspace units; account preferences provide defaults for new documents. Choose a suitable drawing template when creating a drawing, and check that drawing's units and sheet settings too.

  • Confirm the active document or workspace and the tab you are editing.
  • Check length and angle units before entering bare numbers.
  • Enter a known dimension and verify its displayed value and units.
  • Check drawing units and sheet scale separately from the model.

Changing the display from inches to millimeters should express the same physical length in another unit. It does not repair geometry created at the wrong size. Display precision controls how many digits you see; it is not a manufacturing tolerance.

Supporting detail: Addendum 21 — Template and unit references.

Keep referenced files together when you transfer a design; Practice

Keep referenced files together when you transfer a design

For a typical file-based SOLIDWORKS design, the assembly points to component files, and a drawing points to its model. Sending only the assembly file may leave the recipient without the parts. Renaming or moving files outside a reference-aware workflow can break those connections.

Use Pack and Go to gather a design's related files. Review the package contents, including required drawings, then open the transferred design and check for missing references. Files can be reorganized when references are updated; they do not have to remain permanently in the original folder.

Supporting detail: Addendum 22 — Why a folder copy needs checking.

Check file references Choose a tab Check units

Practice choosing a complete reference package; Interactive

Practice choosing a complete reference package

A reference is a stored relationship from one design document to another. In this lesson's declared graph, an arrow A → B means document A requires document B. A drawing may require a model; an assembly may require parts and subassemblies; each subassembly may require more components.

Start with the document you intend to deliver, then follow every required arrow. This is the dependency closure: the starting document plus every directly and transitively required document. A shared component appears once even when two parents require it.

Static worked case — clamp drawing: the drawing requires the clamp assembly. The assembly requires left and right arm subassemblies plus the base. Both arm subassemblies require the same pivot pin, so the complete six-document set contains the pin once.

Available but omitted
The source file exists, but it was not selected for this package. Add the required document.
Unavailable at source
The declared required document cannot be obtained in the scenario. Checking its box cannot create it; locate or restore the actual source first.
Changed symbolic locator
The intended node still has the same stable identity, but one declared edge expects an old locator. Explicitly retarget that edge. A same-looking or same-named substitute is not automatically the intended document.

This graph is a teaching model, not actual CAD file management. It performs no file operations, uploads, downloads, renames, Pack and Go command, cloud lookup, or PDM action. Real CAD systems can use paths, internal identifiers, search locations, platform records, and workflow rules beyond this declared graph.

Use a reference-aware workflow to inspect and collect the real design. In SOLIDWORKS, Find References can list documents referenced by the active file, Pack and Go can gather related files, and File Utilities can update references during supported rename, replace, or move operations. Review the result and open the transferred design to check it.

Supporting detail: Addendum 23 — Why this lab does not imitate a folder copy.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

CAD History, Versions, and Sharing

Separate feature order from edit history, preserve useful design states, and share the intended model with the right access.

The feature list describes how geometry is built

The feature list describes how geometry is built

The SOLIDWORKS FeatureManager design tree and the Onshape feature list help you find sketches and modeling features. Later features can depend on earlier geometry. Rename important features so another reader can tell what they do.

A tree also contains items such as planes, bodies, or components; not every row is a modeling operation. To understand how features build a part, continue with Feature-based Modeling.

A rollback bar lets you work at an earlier position in the feature sequence while later features are temporarily left out of regeneration. Move it forward again to evaluate the complete model and check dependent features. Rolling back does not retrieve an old saved revision, and it is not the same operation as separately suppressing one feature.

Supporting detail: Addendum 24 — Rollback follows the regeneration sequence.

Onshape history records edits; versions preserve milestones; Interactive

Onshape history records edits; versions preserve milestones

Onshape records completed edits in document history. The feature list shows the modeling sequence; history records changes to the document over time. Editing an early sketch today changes the history today even though the sketch remains early in the feature list.

A version captures the design state of the workspace, including its tabs, at a named point. That captured design state is read-only. Use a meaningful milestone name and description so a reviewer knows which state you mean.

A branch starts from a version and provides a separate workspace for further edits. Use it to explore an alternative while preserving the starting version. Compare changes before merging; merging needs review, not just a button click.

Supporting detail: Addendum 25 — Viewing history, restoring, and branching serve different purposes.

Worked symbolic timeline: feature order stays put while edits accumulate

What: the feature list remains Mounting sketch → Base extrude → Edge fillet. Why: editing the first feature later should add a new history event, not move that feature to the end of the regeneration sequence.

  1. Start Main workspace: sketch width 60 mm, extrude depth 12 mm, fillet radius 2 mm.
  2. Edit the early Mounting sketch now: width 60 → 72 mm. It remains feature 1.
  3. Create the fixed Design review snapshot: 72 / 12 / 2 mm.
  4. Edit Main again: sketch width 72 → 84 mm. The snapshot still reads 72 / 12 / 2 mm.
  5. Create Lightweight branch from Design review, then edit only its extrude depth 12 → 8 mm.
  1. 1 · Mounting sketch — width starts at 60 mm.
  2. 2 · Base extrude — depth starts at 12 mm.
  3. 3 · Edge fillet — radius starts at 2 mm.
State after the worked actionsSketch widthExtrude depthFillet radius
Main workspace · editable84 mm12 mm2 mm
Design review · fixed snapshot72 mm12 mm2 mm
Lightweight branch · editable72 mm8 mm2 mm

This is a symbolic in-memory model, not Onshape or SOLIDWORKS. It performs no rollback, restore, merge, save, file operation, or permission change.

A SOLIDWORKS save or file copy needs its own revision plan

A SOLIDWORKS save or file copy needs its own revision plan

In a local file workflow, Save writes the current document to disk. A deliberate copy can preserve an earlier state, but a filename alone does not establish a managed revision or capture all referenced files. Keep descriptive names and know which copy is the active design.

Before copying an assembly or drawing for an alternative, check what its references will point to. Two assembly copies can still use the same part file; editing that shared part can affect both. Use the transfer checks in CAD Files and Documents.

SOLIDWORKS installations may use PDM or connected data management for version and revision control. Follow that system's workflow when present; local Save and Save As are not a universal replacement for it.

Share the intended state and check the recipient's access; Checklist; Practice

Share the intended state and check the recipient's access

In Onshape, decide whether the recipient needs to inspect a fixed version or collaborate in an editable workspace. A link to a changing workspace can show later edits; a version identifies a fixed design state. Grant access using the document's sharing controls.

  • Confirm the document, workspace or version, and tab you intend to share.
  • Review document visibility and the intended recipient.
  • Choose view or edit access and inspect additional permissions such as export, copy, and resharing.
  • Check that the recipient can open the intended state with the intended access.

Do not assume that sending a URL grants access, or that view access prevents copying or exporting. Available sharing options depend on the account and organization. Review Onshape Share Documents for those permissions.

Choose version or branch Distinguish rollback from history Check sharing

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

CAD Model Views and Checks

Navigate a model, choose what edges to show, and check dimensions and mass without changing the design.

Zoom, pan, and rotate change your view of the model

Zoom, pan, and rotate change your view of the model

Zoom changes how large the model appears. Pan shifts it across the window. Rotate orbits the view so you can inspect another side. These viewing operations do not resize the part or move an assembly component.

Use zoom to fit to recover the whole model, zoom to window to enlarge a boxed region, and zoom to selection when you need a selected detail. Mouse buttons, modifier keys, and wheel direction depend on your device and control preferences. Check those settings instead of assuming two platforms use the same gestures.

Use Onshape's view cube or SOLIDWORKS view-orientation controls to return to a known direction. The axis triad helps you keep track of model directions while orbiting.

Normal to looks straight at a selected plane

Normal to looks straight at a selected plane

Front, rear, top, bottom, left, and right are standard model directions. Normal to a planar face or sketch plane means looking along a direction perpendicular to it. An inclined face can therefore have a normal view that is different from every standard view.

Isometric, dimetric, and trimetric are angled parallel-projection views. The three principal axes have equal foreshortening in isometric, two equal in dimetric, and three different in trimetric. Perspective adds apparent size change with distance; turn it off when comparing parallel projected shapes.

Supporting detail: Addendum 26 — Viewing direction is separate from drawing layout.

Choose a display style for the edges you need to inspect

Choose a display style for the edges you need to inspect

Keep the viewing direction fixed while comparing styles. Shading shows surfaces; edge settings decide which boundaries you can see. Labels differ between platforms, so read the option's effect.

Shaded without edges
Filled surfaces emphasize overall form without drawn edge outlines.
Shaded with edges
Filled surfaces plus visible edge outlines make face boundaries easier to follow.
Hidden lines/edges removed
An unshaded view shows visible edges and leaves concealed edges out.
Hidden lines/edges visible
Concealed edges are also shown, distinguished from visible edges. Useful for finding geometry behind the front surface.
Wireframe
Shows the edge framework through the model without opaque shaded faces. Overlapping edges can make depth difficult to read.

Onshape also provides translucent display and shaded display with hidden edges. Translucency lets you see through faces; hidden-edge display highlights concealed boundaries. Neither removes material.

Supporting detail: Addendum 27 — Find the view options in vendor help.

A model section view reveals the inside without cutting the part

A model section view reveals the inside without cutting the part

Use a section view in the model window to clip away the near portion visually. Choose a plane or planar face, set the cut position and direction, and inspect the exposed interior. Turn the section off afterward to see the complete model again.

A viewing section does not create an extruded cut feature. It also does not automatically create a documented section view on a drawing sheet. See Onshape Section View help for the available section controls.

Check the selection before trusting a measurement; Checklist

Check the selection before trusting a measurement

Select the actual entities you need, then use Measure. An edge can provide length; a circular edge can provide radius or diameter; two suitable entities can provide distance or angle. Read the result label: minimum distance, center distance, and distance along an axis answer different questions.

Quick selection properties or status-bar values are useful checks, but they depend on what is selected. A face, an edge, a body, and an assembly component are different selections. Clear old selections before starting a new measurement. Measurement reports geometry; editing a driving dimension changes geometry.

  • Clear the previous selection and select the intended entities.
  • Confirm the highlighted face, edge, or component belongs to the intended part.
  • Read the measurement type and unit with the value.
  • Compare the result with a known dimension or a simple estimate.

Supporting detail: Addendum 28 — Measurement reference.

Mass needs material density as well as geometry; Practice

Mass needs material density as well as geometry

Assign a material to the intended part or body before relying on mass properties. A color or metallic appearance alone is not proof that the material density is correct. Check which bodies or components are included, the units, and any overrides before accepting mass or center of mass.

For a uniform solid, mass = density × volume. A correct volume with the wrong density still gives the wrong mass. Center of mass describes how mass is distributed; it need not lie inside the solid material of a hollow or curved part.

Supporting detail: Addendum 29 — Material assignment and mass-property help.

Choose a display style Check normal to Check a section Check mass Check a selection

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

Creating Drawings from CAD Models

Set up a sheet, place linked model views, add requirements, and check the drawing after every design change.

Choose the model and sheet settings before placing views

Choose the model and sheet settings before placing views

Start with the intended part or assembly and confirm its configuration or version: the selected design variant or saved design state. A drawing of the wrong variant can look convincing and still describe the wrong product. See CAD Files and Documents and CAD History, Versions, and Sharing.

A drawing template supplies starting settings. A sheet format supplies the border and title-block layout. CAD systems package these differently, so inspect the resulting sheet: size, units, projection method, scale, and dimension style all matter.

Use the workflow below as a sequence of tasks. Interface names vary by product and release; these are generic descriptions rather than menu instructions for SOLIDWORKS or Onshape.

Place a base view, then derive aligned projected views; Practice

Place a base view, then derive aligned projected views

Insert a base view from the model, choosing an orientation that communicates the shape clearly. Create projected views from that parent view, maintaining the required alignment and projection arrangement. Leave room for dimensions and notes.

The figure uses third-angle placement only as an example. Follow the drawing's declared projection method. Choose enough views to define the shape; three views are not a requirement for every part. Use Choosing Drawing Views, Section Views, and Auxiliary and Detail Views when ordinary views do not explain a feature clearly.

Choose how to add a related view

Distinguish dimensions that control geometry from dimensions that report it; Practice

Distinguish dimensions that control geometry from dimensions that report it

A driving model dimension controls geometry, such as the length of an extrusion. A dimension created by selecting drawing geometry usually reports that geometry. Changing a displayed label is not a sound way to change the part.

Some CAD workflows import model dimensions into drawings and allow linked edits to affect the model. Check the dimension's type and behavior before editing. Do not assume that all drawing dimensions are editable model controls, or that all are independent annotations.

Select dimensions to communicate manufacturing and inspection requirements, not merely every value used while modeling. Add needed tolerances, material information, and feature notes; CAD does not infer all design requirements from shape. Use Choosing Dimensions and Dimension Anatomy and Placement for the dimensioning method.

Distinguish a dimension from a label

Update linked views and inspect the sheet before release; Checklist; Practice

Update linked views and inspect the sheet before release

Associativity is the connection between a model and the drawing information derived from it. When referenced geometry changes, linked views and dimensions can update to reflect it. Depending on the CAD system, update settings, and referenced version, an explicit update or reference change may be needed.

An update is not a completed review. Deleted or replaced edges can leave dimensions detached from their intended features. Notes can become obsolete. A previously exported PDF stays a snapshot; generate and check a new export after approved changes.

  • Confirm the referenced model, variant, and version, then update or rebuild the drawing as needed.
  • Inspect every affected view for the intended geometry, alignment, and readable line display.
  • Resolve detached dimensions and check that each dimension still refers to the intended feature.
  • Review units, view scales, material, tolerances, and notes for completeness and conflicts.
  • Complete the title block and required revision information; obtain the required review.
  • Export the approved sheets and inspect the actual output for missing views, clipped text, and readability.

See Working Drawings and Title Blocks for identifying the released information.

Supporting detail: Addendum 30 — Find the commands in your CAD version.

Review a model change

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

Extrude and Revolve

Turn a sketch into a straight or rotational solid, and choose an end condition that preserves the intended shape when dimensions change.

Extrude carries a cross-section in a straight direction

Extrude carries a cross-section in a straight direction

For a plain solid extrusion, select a closed sketch region and give it depth. A rectangular region makes a block; a circular region makes a cylinder. Without draft, the cross-section remains constant along the extrusion.

A boss/base extrusion creates or adds solid material. An extruded cut removes material where the extrusion intersects the target solid. Check the arrow, preview, and selected bodies. A cut pointing away from the part cannot remove material from it.

In Onshape, choose the result operation New, Add, or Remove. In SOLIDWORKS, check the boss/cut command and merge or feature scope settings. Adding touching material and creating a separate body are different intentions.

Supporting detail: Addendum 31 — Closed profiles, thin features, and surfaces.

Choose the end condition for what should happen after an edit; Interactive; Practice

Choose the end condition for what should happen after an edit

ConditionWhat controls the endUse when
BlindA specified distance in the selected direction.A pocket must keep a particular depth.
Through allAll target material along the selected direction.A cut must remain through as the part thickens. Check body scope and one- versus two-direction settings.
Up to nextThe next terminating surface that intercepts the entire profile.The next suitable boundary is the intended stop. It is not simply the first edge encountered.
Up to surface / faceA selected terminating surface or face.The feature must follow that particular boundary when it moves. The selection becomes a dependency.
Mid-planeA total depth split equally about the sketch plane.The part must stay centered. In SOLIDWORKS, a 14 mm Mid Plane depth extends 7 mm each way.

Worked thickness edit. One rectangular cut starts on the top face of one flat plate, travels downward normal to that face, and removes material from that selected body only. Compare a distance-controlled blind cut with a through-all cut before and after the plate becomes thicker.

All three sections use the same vertical scale: 8 drawing units per millimeter.

Design goalChoice that survives the editWhy
Opening must stay throughThrough allThe termination follows the selected plate thickness.
Pocket must retain a floorBlind, with a depth smaller than the final thicknessThe fixed distance intentionally stops before the far face.

This teaching model does not cover up-to-face, up-to-next, multiple bodies, opposite directions or revolved cuts. Check the selected sketch region, direction and body scope in the CAD preview.

Do not substitute an oversized blind cut for a through-all requirement. It may work today and leave a thin floor after a later edit. Conversely, through all is wrong for a pocket that must retain its floor.

Onshape uses a Symmetric option for supported end types. Dialog names and available conditions depend on the selected operation; inspect the preview and measured result rather than transferring every setting by name.

Practice end conditions Practice symmetric depth

Supporting detail: Addendum 32 — Vendor help for extrusion boundaries.

Revolve rotates a section around an axis

Revolve rotates a section around an axis

Select a section, an axis of rotation, and an angle. A full turn is 360°; a smaller angle produces a partial rotational shape. A boss revolve adds material, and a revolved cut removes it. Start with a closed section on one side of the axis for a straightforward solid revolve.

A straight sketch line, centerline, or reference axis can define rotation when supported by the command. The axis must be deliberately located. A diameter describes the distance across a round shape; the distance from the axis to its outer wall is the radius.

A stepped sleeve can often be built with one revolved section including its bore. Repeated extrusions and cuts can also build it, but put the coaxial steps under separate controls. Choose the sequence that makes the important dimensions easiest to change.

Supporting detail: Addendum 33 — Check overlap and axis selection before adding complexity.

Pick the base feature from the shape's main organizing rule; Practice

Pick the base feature from the shape's main organizing rule

Use extrusion when a useful section stays the same along a straight direction. Use revolution when a useful section repeats around an axis. A cylinder can be made either way. A rotationally stepped part often makes the reason for choosing revolve clearer than a plain cylinder does.

Before accepting either feature, confirm the profile, direction or axis, end condition or angle, and result body. Then make one trial dimension change. Does the model still express the intent described in Feature-based Modeling?

Practice choosing a base Practice a scoped feature count

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

Feature-based Modeling

Plan a solid part as a sequence of features, choose stable references, and test whether the model survives a change.

Build the main shape, then add and remove material

Build the main shape, then add and remove material

A parametric model stores instructions for building a shape. Dimensions and relationships are inputs; the solid is the result. Change an input and rebuild to see the result update.

The base feature creates the initial solid. Later features add material, remove material, or modify faces and edges. For a simple spacer, start with its main cross-section and extrude it. For a stepped round knob, a revolved section may describe the main shape more directly. There is often more than one valid feature sequence.

A body is a connected piece of solid geometry. A SOLIDWORKS part file can contain multiple bodies. An Onshape Part Studio can create multiple parts from a shared feature list. Neither arrangement, by itself, defines assembly motion or assembly relationships.

Start with sketch dimensions and relations in the Engineering Graphics collection. Then choose extrude or revolve for a straight or rotational shape, or sweep or loft for a path or a changing cross-section.

The feature tree records a build sequence and its dependencies

The feature tree records a build sequence and its dependencies

Read the tree from the base feature toward the end. A feature that supplies a sketch, face, edge, or other reference is a parent; a feature that uses that reference is a child. A child can depend on more than one parent. Being later in the list does not, by itself, make a feature a direct child of every earlier feature.

For example: a plate extrusion supplies a top face for a hole-position sketch. A hole feature uses that sketch. A pattern uses that hole as its seed. Delete the hole and the pattern loses its seed; delete the plate and the sketch loses its support as well. Inspect the deletion dialog before accepting dependent deletions.

Rename features for their purpose, such as Main plate, Locating hole, and Hole row. Renaming a feature in the tree is different from renaming a referenced part file. File references need their own reference-aware workflow.

Supporting detail: Addendum 34 — Why a small edit can break a later feature.

Rollback lets you inspect an earlier stage without deleting later work; Checklist

Rollback lets you inspect an earlier stage without deleting later work

Move the rollback bar above later features to inspect or edit an earlier stage. Return it to the end when checking the completed part. Rollback is a temporary stopping point in regeneration. Suppression instead leaves a selected feature in the tree but excludes it from the active model; dependent features may also be affected. Hiding changes visibility, not the solid's definition.

  • Find the earliest feature that fails or produces the wrong shape.
  • Roll back to inspect the geometry and references available at that point.
  • Edit the sketch for its dimensions or relations; edit the feature for its operation, depth, direction, or selected references.
  • Roll forward to the end, rebuild, and inspect the downstream results.

Supporting detail: Addendum 35 — Vendor help for history and rollback.

Choose references that express what must stay aligned

Choose references that express what must stay aligned

A reference plane locates a sketch or defines symmetry. A reference axis supplies a direction or center of rotation. Neither adds material. Use the origin and default planes when they express the design; add offset, angled, or mid-planes when needed. Reference geometry can also have parents.

Design intent is what should stay true when dimensions change. A centered plate should grow equally on both sides of its center plane. A hole required to pass through the plate should remain through when the plate gets thicker. A row of identical holes should share one seed definition and a spacing rule.

Put major shape and functional references early. Add small edge treatments later when they are finishing details. This is a useful starting order, not a rule that every fillet must be last: a large blend that defines the main shape may belong before shelling or other features.

Supporting detail: Addendum 36 — Fewest features is not always the best model.

Check units, bodies, material, and mass after a change; Checklist; Practice

Check units, bodies, material, and mass after a change

Assign the intended material or density before relying on mass. A surface color is not evidence that density is correct. For a uniform solid, mass = density × volume. Compare volume with a simple estimate, and inspect unexpected mass or center-of-mass changes.

A fresh example: a solid rectangular spacer measuring 30 × 20 × 8 mm has a volume of 4,800 mm³ = 4.8 cm³. With an assumed density of 2.50 g/cm³, its mass is 12.0 g. These are practice values, not a material specification. A hole should reduce that mass if the same body and density remain selected.

  • Confirm the document units and overall dimensions.
  • Confirm the expected body or part count and the scope of each add or cut.
  • Change one important dimension, rebuild, and check the intended relationships.
  • Check material assignment, selected bodies, and any mass overrides before trusting the result.

Practice a mass check Practice dependencies

Supporting detail: Addendum 37 — Mass properties are a check, not proof of a correct part.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

Fully Defined Sketches and Design Intent

Remove unwanted freedom with relations and dimensions, then test whether edits preserve the intended shape.

Predict how an anchored rectangle grows, then test its remaining motion; Interactive; Practice

Predict how an anchored rectangle grows, then test its remaining motion

Rectangle constraint lab. Start with a 64 × 22 mm rectangular label blank. Predict where its left and right edges will be when the driving width changes to 80 mm. Compare a lower-left corner at the origin with a center at the origin.

Width changes from 64 to 80 mm; both sketches are fully defined before and after
Origin choiceLeft x (mm)Right x (mm)Free motion
Lower-left corner0 → 064 → 800 DOF
Center−32 → −4032 → 400 DOF

Diagnose the freedom: keep width and height driving, but remove only the horizontal anchor. The rectangle can translate horizontally: 1 DOF remains. Remove the width instead while retaining both anchors and height; the corner-anchored rectangle's right edge can move, or the centered rectangle can grow symmetrically. Restore the conditions before testing the intended size edit.

Measure versus constrain: a top-edge reference dimension reports the current width and adds no equation. A second driving width that agrees with the first repeats the same equation: five displayed conditions can still have only four independent conditions. A different second driving width contradicts the first; there is no feasible rectangle, so the lab retains its last valid drawing rather than displaying an invented solution.

Bounded model: one closed axis-aligned rectangle, with four variables [left x, right x, bottom y, top y]. Closure, rectangular shape and orientation are built in. For a feasible set, DOF = 4 − rank (the independent equation count). Width and height stay between 1 and 120 mm; these bounds restrict admissible sizes and do not count as equality constraints. The lab projects toward the nearest solution of the active equalities and rejects changes outside its size range. It models no rotation or other sketch entities and does not reproduce a vendor's solver or error colors.

With JavaScript enabled, use the prediction, size controls and two draggable corners. Keyboard: focus a corner and press arrow keys; Shift changes the requested step from 1 to 5 mm. Undo diagnostic motion restores the previous drawing.

Practice: predict centered growth Practice: reference dimensions and freedom

Count independent ways the geometry can still change

Count independent ways the geometry can still change

A degree of freedom (DOF) is one independent variable still available to change. Constraints remove freedom. Count the geometry's possible motion, not the number of icons.

Simple, isolated 2D entities before any dimensions or relations
EntityFree variablesDOF
Pointx and y position2
Nonzero line segmentx and y for each endpoint4
CircleCenter x, center y, radius3
Circular arcCenter x, center y, radius, two endpoint angles5

A circle's diameter dimension removes one DOF; its center can still move in two directions. Making its center coincident with the origin removes those two. A line with one endpoint at the origin still has length and direction to determine.

Supporting detail: Addendum 38 — Why subtracting one per relation gives wrong answers.

A driving dimension controls size; a driven dimension reports it

A driving dimension controls size; a driven dimension reports it

A driving dimension is a constraint: changing its value asks the solver to change the geometry while keeping the other rules. Length, angle, radius, diameter, and location dimensions can all supply constraints.

A driven or reference dimension measures a result already controlled elsewhere. It does not remove another DOF. For example, a circle whose size is set by a 24 mm driving diameter already has a 12 mm radius; a second driving radius dimension duplicates that control.

Use a relation for an enduring geometric rule and a dimension for the independent value you intend to change. Two lengths that must remain equal need an equal relation and one driving length, rather than two unrelated numbers that happen to match today.

Onshape automatically makes a newly added dimension driven if it would over-define the sketch. Check whether a displayed value is driving before expecting it to control geometry.

Supporting detail: Addendum 39 — Software treatment of redundant dimensions.

For drawing presentation and dimension placement, see Dimension Anatomy and Placement.

Read the sketch state in the software you are using

Read the sketch state in the software you are using

  • Under-defined / underconstrained: some position, orientation, or size remains free.
  • Fully defined / fully constrained: no free motion remains with the current driving values. Editing those values can still change the sketch.
  • Over-defined / overconstrained: dimensions or relations conflict or add control the solver treats as redundant. Repair the conflicting set.
Documented colors for sketch geometry while editing; selection and hover highlighting are separate
SoftwareUnder-definedFully definedProblems
SOLIDWORKS 2026BlueBlackGeometry-status help identifies yellow for conflicting or invalid items and red for unsolvable items; a redundant driving dimension can be red.
OnshapeBlueBlackRed geometry indicates a constraint problem. A problem constraint icon is white on red.

Read status messages and inspect relations as well as color. One black edge does not prove that the entire sketch is fully defined. An under-defined construction line or endpoint can be easy to overlook.

Supporting detail: Addendum 40 — Current vendor references for status colors.

Fully define a sketch in a repeatable order; Checklist

Fully define a sketch in a repeatable order

  • State what must stay aligned, centered, equal, or tangent when the size changes.
  • Choose the plane and an origin reference that suit that intent. Confirm the working units.
  • Draw the simplest useful entities. Check the automatic relations and remove unintended ones.
  • Connect the intended endpoints and apply the geometric relations that describe the shape.
  • Anchor the sketch's position to the origin or other stable references; control its orientation.
  • Add independent driving dimensions for the remaining sizes and locations.
  • Inspect the remaining free points and curves. Drag gently to diagnose motion, then undo the diagnostic move.
  • Resolve conflicts before adding more constraints. Inspect the whole sketch, including construction geometry.
  • Change one intended driving value, check that the sketch behaves correctly, then restore the value.

Fully defined is a useful check, not proof of good design intent. Fixing a misplaced point can remove freedom without giving it the correct location. A sketch can be completely constrained by dimensions that make future edits awkward.

Test design intent with a change, not just the starting shape; Practice

Test design intent with a change, not just the starting shape

Fresh practice part: a circular inspection plate. Sketch two circular boundaries for an annular plate. Put their common center at the origin; use concentric and separate diameter dimensions of 46 mm and 18 mm. Increasing the outer diameter to 58 mm should leave the inner opening centered and unchanged in size.

Fresh practice part: a rectangular label blank. Use an axis-aligned rectangle with its lower-left corner at the origin, width 64 mm, and height 22 mm. Increasing the width to 80 mm should move the right edge while the left edge stays at the origin. If the intended part must grow equally left and right, choose a centered construction instead.

These two origin choices describe different editing behavior. There is no single best anchor for every part. Decide what should stay put before dimensioning.

Practice: count remaining freedom Practice: spot duplicate control

Repair the unwanted rule, then check the intended change again

Repair the unwanted rule, then check the intended change again

When an added dimension causes an error, inspect what already controls that measurement. Keep the relation or dimension that expresses the intended design. Remove the duplicate, or make a measurement driven if it is only there to report a result.

A horizontal line cannot also have a nonzero vertical separation between its endpoints. Equal circles cannot have different driving diameters. These are contradictions; adding still more dimensions will not solve them.

SOLIDWORKS offers Display/Delete Relations and SketchXpert for diagnosis. Onshape's Constraint manager filters constraints and dimensions to help locate problems. A suggested deletion is still a design decision: check what behavior you would lose.

Supporting detail: Addendum 41 — Redundancy is not the same as contradiction.

Return to Geometric Relations in Sketches to compare rules, or Sketch Entities and Planes to review the geometry they act on.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

Geometric Relations in Sketches

Match each relation to the motion it prevents, and distinguish shared position, direction, size, and curvature.

Relations preserve geometry when dimensions change

Relations preserve geometry when dimensions change

A geometric relation is a rule the sketch must continue to satisfy: two lines stay parallel, two circles keep one center, or an endpoint stays on a curve. Onshape generally calls these rules constraints; SOLIDWORKS calls them relations.

Choose the entities carefully. Selecting a circle's center is different from selecting its circumference. A relation can remove some motion while leaving other motion available. The diagrams show only the named rule, not a complete dimensioning scheme.

The before/after drawings are original geometry diagrams, not software icons. Their line colors do not indicate sketch status.

Coincident connects a point; midpoint puts it halfway along

Coincident connects a point; midpoint puts it halfway along

Coincident

Two points share a location, or a point lies on a selected line or curve. Joining two endpoints closes their gap. A point on a line can still slide along it unless another rule locates it.

Midpoint

A point stays halfway between a segment's endpoints. It is more specific than simply putting the point somewhere on the line. Onshape also supports midpoint on an arc.

Supporting detail: Addendum 42 — Point selection and vendor names.

Collinear shares a line; parallel shares only its direction

Collinear shares a line; parallel shares only its direction

Collinear

Two straight segments lie on the same infinite line. They may have a gap between them; collinear does not join their endpoints.

Parallel

Two lines keep the same direction. Their spacing, lengths, and positions along that direction still need other rules.

Software vocabulary: SOLIDWORKS has a Collinear relation. Onshape's documented toolbar has no separate Collinear entry. For two nonzero straight segments, placing both endpoints of one coincident with the other's underlying line enforces the same geometric condition. This is a construction from point-on-line constraints, not an Onshape command name.

Horizontal and vertical use the axes; perpendicular uses another line

Horizontal and vertical use the axes; perpendicular uses another line

Horizontal

A line's endpoints have the same vertical coordinate. For two selected points, horizontal aligns their heights without joining them.

Vertical

A line's endpoints have the same horizontal coordinate. Two selected points can likewise be aligned vertically.

Perpendicular

Two line directions form a right angle. They may rotate together while preserving that angle. The relation does not require their finite segments to meet.

Supporting detail: Addendum 43 — Why horizontal plus vertical can already supply a right angle.

Concentric shares a center; equal shares size; coradial shares both

Concentric shares a center; equal shares size; coradial shares both

Concentric

Circles or circular arcs share a center. They can have different radii. For arcs, their endpoints and sweep angles are not determined by this relation.

Equal

Selected line segments keep equal lengths; selected circles or circular arcs keep equal radii. Equal does not move their centers together. Equal arc radii do not imply equal arc lengths when the sweep angles differ.

Coradial

Two circular arcs share both center and radius: they belong to the same underlying circle. They need not touch or have equal sweep angles. SOLIDWORKS names this relation Coradial. In Onshape, concentric plus equal radius expresses this condition.

Supporting detail: Addendum 44 — Check the circular relation definitions.

Tangent controls direction at contact; Fix holds a reference in place

Tangent controls direction at contact; Fix holds a reference in place

Tangent

A line and a circle touch without crossing: the line is perpendicular to the radius at contact. Curves meeting tangentially have a common tangent direction. Tangency alone does not necessarily join the endpoints you intended; add endpoint coincidence when a continuous profile needs it.

Fix

Fix grounds selected geometry at its current location. Fixing a point removes its freedom to move in the sketch plane. It is useful for a deliberate fixed reference, but does not explain why an arbitrary location or size is correct.

SOLIDWORKS qualification: its relation reference says endpoints of a fixed line can still move along the underlying infinite line, and arc endpoints can move along the supporting circle. Check the entity and its endpoints. Onshape describes Fix as grounding the selected entity on the sketch plane.

Supporting detail: Addendum 45 — Vendor help for tangent and fixed geometry.

Watch automatic relations, then check what was stored; Practice

Watch automatic relations, then check what was stored

Sketching tools can add relations while you draw. A visual alignment is useful feedback; inspect the resulting relation icons before assuming the intended rule is present.

  • SOLIDWORKS: with Automatic Relations enabled, its documented cursor cues include horizontal, vertical, coincident, midpoint, perpendicular, and tangent. Hold Ctrl while sketching to suppress automatic relations temporarily.
  • Onshape: Automatic Inferencing documents horizontal, vertical, midpoint, parallel, and coincident as common inferences. Hover near existing geometry to activate the relevant inference; Shift suppresses inferencing while dragging.

These are documented examples, not an exhaustive promise for every tool. For equal, concentric, coradial, collinear, or fix, deliberately apply or verify the required rule. Rectangle, slot, and other creation tools can supply their own relations.

If an unwanted rule was stored, remove that specific rule before adding a conflicting dimension. Continue with Fully Defined Sketches and Design Intent.

Supporting detail: Addendum 46 — Automatic behavior depends on the tool and settings.

Practice: distinguish circular relations

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

Patterns, Mirror, and Applied Features

Repeat geometry with a rule, model useful hole information, and finish a solid with edge treatments, shell, draft, and ribs.

Pattern a seed when the copies should change together; Practice

Pattern a seed when the copies should change together

A seed is the original feature being repeated. A feature pattern makes the repetition explicit: edit the seed's size once and rebuild the copies. Model independent features when their sizes or locations must change independently.

A linear pattern uses a direction, spacing, and count. For a single-direction row with N total instances including the seed, the distance from first center to last is (N − 1) × spacing. Some dialogs also offer a total-span mode; check which distance the field means.

A circular pattern repeats around an axis. N evenly spaced instances around a complete circle have an angular pitch of 360°/N. A partial arc with both endpoints occupied instead has N − 1 intervals across that arc. Inspect whether the dialog asks for total angle or angle between instances.

Choose feature, face, or body/part pattern deliberately. A feature pattern repeats selected operations; a body/part pattern repeats a larger solid. Check target bodies, skipped instances, and whether every copy actually intersects the intended material.

Supporting detail: Addendum 47 — Copied geometry and recalculated end conditions can differ.

Practice linear spacing Practice angular spacing

Mirror across a plane when symmetry is the rule; Practice

Mirror across a plane when symmetry is the rule

A mirror reflects selected features or bodies across a plane. Corresponding points lie at equal distances on opposite sides. It is not a rotation: an asymmetric shape changes handedness.

A stable center plane is usually a better symmetry reference than a face likely to move independently. Check whether the mirror should join material into one body or create another. Assemblies use separate tools to position components; part-level mirror features do not define assembly motion.

See Onshape: Mirror for selection and result options.

Practice symmetry

Hole features store type and size as well as position

Hole features store type and size as well as position

Use a hole feature when the hole needs structured information such as a fastener size, fit, counterbore, countersink, or tapped-hole specification. A counterbore is a larger cylindrical recess; a countersink is a conical recess. A plain circular cut can make geometry, but does not automatically carry the same hole definition.

In SOLIDWORKS Hole Wizard, use Type for the hole parameters and Positions for its centers. Select the appropriate standard, type, size, fit where offered, and end condition. Locate the centers with dimensions and relations. Different hole types require separate Hole Wizard features.

For tapped holes, distinguish drill depth from thread depth. A cosmetic thread represents thread information without cutting a helical groove in the solid. Inspect the selected thread option before expecting detailed thread geometry in an export.

Read hole callouts and drawing symbols in the Engineering Graphics dimensioning topics. This page covers the model feature, not callout syntax.

Supporting detail: Addendum 48 — Hole options depend on type and software version.

Fillet rounds an edge; chamfer bevels it

Fillet rounds an edge; chamfer bevels it

A fillet creates a rounded transition. A chamfer creates a beveled transition. Select the intended edges, set the radius or chamfer dimensions, and inspect the preview all the way around the selection. A small radius can still fail where neighboring faces leave too little room.

Keep edge treatments separate when they have different functions or are likely to change independently. Cosmetic edge breaks often belong late; a large blend that controls the main shape may belong early. See planning feature order.

Shell hollows a solid and leaves a controlled wall; Practice

Shell hollows a solid and leaves a controlled wall

Select faces to remove and specify the remaining wall thickness. Removing the top face of a block makes an open container; keeping all faces can make an enclosed cavity. Check whether the thickness is offset inward or outward.

If shell fails, inspect small radii and narrow regions where offset faces collide. Try a simpler outer shape or revisit the intended thickness. Do not silently reduce a required wall just to make the command succeed. See Onshape: Shell.

Practice hollowing a part

Draft tapers faces; a rib adds a thin support; Practice

Draft tapers faces; a rib adds a thin support

Draft inclines faces relative to a pull direction, often to help a molded part release. In a neutral-plane construction, that reference keeps its size while selected side faces tilt. Check the direction and which end grows or shrinks. There is no universal draft angle for every material and process.

A rib adds a thin web between supporting regions. It usually starts from sketch curves plus a thickness and direction. Although grouped here with finishing features, a rib needs sketch geometry. Check that it meets the intended walls and merges with the intended part.

See Onshape: Draft, Rib, and the feature tool glossary. After any applied feature, rebuild, inspect the section, and make a trial change to its parent geometry.

Practice support features Practice draft

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

Sketch Entities and Planes

Choose where a 2D sketch lives, then build its shape from simple entities and construction geometry.

Choose the sketch plane before drawing the shape

Choose the sketch plane before drawing the shape

A 2D sketch is a set of points and curves on one plane. The plane places the sketch in the model; the sketch's origin and axes give you references for locating its geometry.

  • Standard plane: Front, Top, or Right is a useful starting reference for a new part. Choose the view that makes the intended profile easiest to describe.
  • Model face: use an existing planar face when the new sketch belongs on that face. A curved face is not itself a 2D sketch plane.
  • Reference plane: an added plane can locate a sketch where the standard planes and existing faces do not.

The origin is a point, not a plane. Starting a line or circle at the origin can anchor its position, but you still need a sketch plane. You may start elsewhere when that suits the design; then constrain the location relative to a deliberate reference.

Look normal to the sketch plane: straight at it, rather than at an angle. Horizontal and vertical refer to the sketch's axes, even when you rotate the model on screen.

Supporting detail: Addendum 49 — Sketch placement in Onshape.

Use the simplest entity that describes the shape

Use the simplest entity that describes the shape

Sketch entities and the information they need
EntityWhat it describesWhat to control
LineA straight segment between two endpoints.Position, direction, and length.
CircleA complete round curve.Center position and radius or diameter.
ArcPart of a circle.Center, radius, and where the arc begins and ends.
RectangleFour connected lines with right-angle corners.Position, orientation, width, and height. Tool-created relations often supply some of these.
SlotA constant-width path with rounded ends. A simple straight slot has two parallel sides and two semicircular ends.Path position and direction, width, and length. State whether length means overall length or distance between end centers.
SplineA curve shaped by fit points or control points and handles.Point locations and curve shape. Use it when a line or circular arc cannot express the intended contour.

Rectangle and slot tools create useful groups of geometry. They do not guarantee that the resulting sketch is fully defined. Inspect their relations before adding more.

Supporting detail: Addendum 50 — Find the tools by their software names.

Construction geometry guides the sketch without outlining material

Construction geometry guides the sketch without outlining material

A centerline is a common use of construction geometry: a reference for a center, symmetry, angle, or axis. Construction geometry participates in dimensions and relations, but does not serve as the ordinary boundary of a filled profile.

In SOLIDWORKS, Centerline creates construction geometry. In Onshape, use Construction to toggle selected sketch entities or to create construction geometry. Use a construction circle for a layout circle just as you would use a construction line for an axis.

Supporting detail: Addendum 51 — Vendor reference for construction geometry.

Check connections before moving on to a feature; Practice

Check connections before moving on to a feature

Two endpoints that look joined may still be separate. A tiny gap can prevent a profile from closing. Use a coincident relation to make the connection intentional, then inspect the sketch.

Closed and fully defined are different checks. A closed circle can still move or change size. A fully defined chain of lines can still be open. Later features such as extrude or revolve use sketches in different ways; choose the profile that the intended feature needs.

Continue with Geometric Relations in Sketches and Fully Defined Sketches and Design Intent. For view interpretation, see Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box; for drawing dimensions, see Dimension Anatomy and Placement.

Practice: choose a sketch reference

Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling

Sweeps and Lofts

Use a sweep to carry a section along a path and a loft to transition through ordered sections, with references that control the result.

A sweep needs a profile and a path

A sweep needs a profile and a path

A profile describes the cross-section; a path describes where it travels. A circular profile swept around a smooth bend makes a bent solid rod. An annular profile can make a tube. For a basic sweep, keep the section size constant and choose how it stays oriented along the path.

Place the profile on a plane normal (perpendicular) to the path at its start for an easy first construction. Constrain its position to the path. A shape that looks connected in one view can still be separated in three dimensions. Select the complete intended path, not a neighboring model edge.

A sweep can create material or remove it from an existing part. Advanced sweep options can control twist or scaling; a constant circular section is a simpler starting case. See Onshape: Sweep.

Sweep lab: how tight can a bend be before a thick profile folds?; Interactive

Sweep lab: how tight can a bend be before a thick profile folds?

Choose a profile and a path, then tighten the bend. Watch where the inside of the sweep turns red: there, the profile reaches the centre of the bend and the inner wall has to fold back through itself.

The rule this lab tests. Carry a profile along a path. At each point the path has a bend radius ρ: the radius of the circle that best fits the path there, measured to its centre of curvature. The profile also has a reach toward that centre: how far its edge extends from the path toward the inside of the bend. The inner wall folds through itself where

reach toward the centre of curvature ≥ local bend radius ρ

For a round rod centred on the path, the reach is its radius, so a rod of diameter D fails around a bend when D/2 ≥ ρ. Exactly equal is already a failure: the inner wall shrinks to an edge at the centre of curvature.

Profile on a 12 mm arcReach toward centreResult
Ø16 mm rod8 mmBuilds (8 < 12)
Ø24 mm rod12 mmFails: inner wall collapses to an edge (12 = 12)
Ø30 mm rod15 mmFails: folds (15 > 12)
30 × 15 mm bar, 30 mm side across the bend15 mmFails: folds
Same bar turned, 15 mm side across the bend7.5 mmBuilds

Only the local bend matters for this test. On an S-curve the bend radius changes along the path, so the failure appears only near the tightest bends. Here a Ø20 mm rod (reach 10 mm) follows an S-curve whose tightest bend radius is 8 mm: 6% of the path fails.

A passing local test is not a complete check. This lab calls a sweep “builds” only on the U-bend, where the geometry also rules out clashes; anywhere else a passing local test is reported as only that, with global clearance not established. A Ø20 mm wire wound with a 30 mm coil radius bends gently (bend radius 30.2 mm), but with a 16 mm pitch neighbouring turns are only 15.9 mm apart, so the wire hits the next coil. Coils collide: neighbouring turns are 15.94 mm apart along the chord between them, but the profile needs 20 mm. The local bend test cannot see this clash.

Teaching model: the profile is centred on the path and carried without avoidable twist (a rotation-minimising frame). The red regions come from the local test only. It is not a complete validity check. The helix chord check can prove that neighbouring coils collide, never that they clear. A given CAD product may report failures differently or offer other orientation options. Sources: Patrikalakis, Maekawa and Cho, Local self-intersection of pipe surfaces and Global self-intersection of pipe surfaces; Onshape: Sweep.

A loft passes through profiles selected in order

A loft passes through profiles selected in order

A loft transitions between two or more sections. Put sketches on suitable planes, then select the sections in the order the shape should pass through them. A broad oval transitioning to a smaller oval is a simple example; the section size changes along the length.

Use a guide curve when the profiles alone do not control the shape between them. For a straightforward boundary guide, constrain it to meet every profile at the intended boundary point. A Pierce relation can locate a sketch point where a curve crosses that sketch plane. Do not accept a connection solely because it looks right in an isometric view.

Match corresponding locations around successive profiles. If one section's corner connects to an unrelated corner on the next, the loft can twist. Inspect connection handles and a section view before adding more profiles.

Supporting detail: Addendum 52 — More profiles do not automatically make a better surface.

Loft lab: what moving a start point or reordering profiles does; Interactive

Loft lab: what moving a start point or reordering profiles does

Three profiles stay in place: a square, a circle and a slot. Change only which points the loft pairs and the order you select the profiles, then watch the connector lines twist, pinch or double back.

What decides a loft’s shape. Each profile is divided into the same number of points, counted from its start point (the connector) in the same direction. Point 1 of the first profile joins point 1 of the next, and so on; the loft passes through the profiles in the order selected. Three profiles sit on parallel planes: a 60 mm square at the bottom, a Ø44 mm circle 45 mm up, and a 56 × 24 mm slot at 90 mm.

ChangeResultFix
Start points do not correspondTwist; a large mismatch pinches or crosses itselfLine up the connectors or start points
Profiles selected out of their order along the partLoft doubles back across heights already occupiedSelect profiles in sequence
Whole selection reversedSame surface, built from the other endNothing to fix

Teaching model: every profile runs counter-clockwise, and corresponding points are joined by a smooth curve through all three profiles. A profile drawn in the opposite direction is a separate problem, not modelled here. Twist and crossing come from the actual sections. Source: Onshape: Loft (sequential profile order; connections control twist).

Use the controlling geometry to choose sweep or loft; Practice

Use the controlling geometry to choose sweep or loft

What you knowFirst feature to considerWhat to inspect
One section following a bent centerlineSweepPath continuity, section position, and orientation.
Different sections at several locationsLoftProfile order, connections, and shape between sections.
One section along a straight directionExtrudeDepth or end condition.
A section repeated around an axisRevolveAxis position and rotation angle.

These are starting choices, not exclusive capabilities. For example, a loft can follow a centerline, and a sweep can vary with advanced controls. Prefer the feature that states the intended change clearly.

Practice profile and path Practice changing sections

Challenge: choose the feature, then the one input that fixes it; Interactive

Challenge: choose the feature, then the one input that fixes it

Each target below comes with a failing attempt. Name the feature that states the shape, then pick the change that makes the attempt match the target.

Choose the feature, then the input to change. For each target, decide whether a sweep, loft or extrude states it, then which change fixes the failing attempt.

  1. U-shaped handrail. One Ø20 mm round section follows a U-shaped centreline with a 30 mm bend radius. Current attempt: fails: the inner wall folds through itself.

    Answer

    Sweep. Yes: one constant section follows a bent centreline, which is what a sweep states. Change: Open the bend radius to 30 mm.

  2. Square-to-round duct transition. A duct changes from a 60 mm square, through a Ø44 mm circle, to a 56 × 24 mm slot, with straight, untwisted sides. Current attempt: twisted: no crossing section found.

    Answer

    Loft. Yes: the section changes shape at known positions, which is what a loft states. Change: Move the circle’s start point back to 0° so it lines up with the square and slot.

  3. Three-section transition built out of order. The same square → circle → slot duct, built bottom to top. Current attempt: wrong shape: the loft doubles back.

    Answer

    Loft. Yes: three different sections at fixed heights. Change: Select square, circle, slot: the order the profiles sit along the part.

  4. Compression spring. Ø16 mm round wire wound with a 24 mm coil radius and a 28 mm pitch. Current attempt: fails: neighbouring coils collide.

    Answer

    Sweep. Yes: one wire section follows a helical path. Change: Increase the pitch to 28 mm.

Troubleshoot the inputs before changing every option; Checklist

Troubleshoot the inputs before changing every option

  • Check that the selected profile regions match the intended solid, surface, or thin result.
  • For a sweep, check path continuity and the profile's location and orientation.
  • For a loft, check profile order and each intended guide intersection.
  • Look for self-intersection: a thick swept section may overlap itself around a tight bend.
  • Inspect sections and confirm the expected part count; repair the first failed reference.

Shelling a complicated loft is a separate geometry problem: offset walls can collide where the shape becomes tight. Build and inspect the outer shape first, then check the wall thickness. See shell and other applied features.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies

Assembly Files and Mates

Keep component references intact and choose mates that locate parts while preserving their intended motion.

An assembly records which parts belong together and how they fit

An assembly records which parts belong together and how they fit

A part defines a component's shape. An assembly places instances of parts and subassemblies and records relationships between them. Two instances of one part can occupy different positions while using the same part definition.

In a file-based SOLIDWORKS assembly, the .SLDASM normally references external .SLDPRT and other assembly files. An assembly drawing references the assembly. Sending only the assembly file can leave the recipient without its components. Virtual components are an exception: their definitions can be stored inside the assembly.

Onshape organizes Part Studios, Assemblies, and Drawings as tabs in documents. Inserted instances reference their source definitions; a tab name is not a Windows filename. Share the document with the appropriate access and identify the intended version when a fixed design state matters.

Supporting detail: Addendum 53 — Definitions, instances, and design changes.

Rename and package files with their references; Checklist

Rename and package files with their references

Renaming or moving a component in ordinary File Explorer can leave an assembly looking for its old name or location. Use the CAD system's reference-aware rename or move workflow. Changing a display name in the tree is not necessarily changing the file name.

  • Save a recoverable copy before reorganizing an assembly's files.
  • Use the supported rename workflow, include affected assemblies and drawings, and save the referencing documents.
  • For file-based SOLIDWORKS sharing, use Pack and Go where available. Review the file list, drawing inclusion, library components, and destination.
  • Open the packaged assembly from its destination and inspect the resolved reference paths. Confirm it is not quietly loading parts from the original folders.

Supporting detail: Addendum 54 — Vendor help for renaming and sharing.

Ground a base, then count the motion you intend to keep

Ground a base, then count the motion you intend to keep

A free rigid component in three-dimensional space has six degrees of freedom (DOF): translation along three axes and rotation about three axes. A degree of freedom is an independent motion, not a count of arrows or mates.

Choose a base or housing as the reference. Fix it, or fully locate it to the assembly origin and planes. In SOLIDWORKS, insertion options include fixing only the first component, fixing inserted components, or leaving them floating. Check the actual state; do not assume that the first component is always fixed. Fixing a base away from the origin holds it there; it does not move it to the origin.

A lever should still rotate about its pivot. A cover should stay put. Fully locating every moving part would turn a mechanism into a rigid model.

Supporting detail: Addendum 55 — Check the insertion setting.

Use geometric mates to describe the intended contact

Use geometric mates to describe the intended contact

Select the actual locating faces, axes, or reference planes. The same mate name can accept different geometry, so its effect depends on what you select. The diagrams below are schematic before/after comparisons, not complete constraints for whole assemblies.

Coincident
For two planar faces, put their supporting planes together. The faces can still slide in that plane and rotate about its normal. Coincident planes do not guarantee that finite faces overlap.
Concentric
Put two cylindrical axes on the same line. Without a rotation lock or other mates, a shaft can still slide along and rotate about that line.

Supporting detail: Addendum 56 — Why subtracting one DOF per mate gives the wrong answer.

Test a shaft joint: keep the motion the design needs; Interactive; Practice

Test a shaft joint: keep the motion the design needs

The housing is grounded. The shaft and its attached lever start with their axes aligned to the housing bore. Predict the motions left, test them, then seat the shoulder. Finally add angular alignment: does a hinge still work?

Worked experiment: 2 → 1 → 0 independent motions

This original ideal joint begins after axis alignment, not as a free rigid body. Its only coordinates are axial position z in millimeters and spin θ in degrees. The housing is grounded; the lever moves with the shaft.

Conditions remove independent motions, not one freedom per mate icon
Condition after built-in axis alignmentExample coordinatesWhat can move?
Neither additional conditionz = 12 mm, θ = 35° → test: 22 mm, 65°Slide + spin: 2 DOF
Seat shoulder at z = 0z = 0 mm, θ = 65°Spin only: 1 DOF. Hinge goal met.
Also align lever at θ = 0°z = 0 mm, θ = 0°Neither: 0 DOF. Fixed goal met; hinge goal defeated.
Angular alignment onlyz may vary, θ = 0°Slide only: 1 DOF. Slider goal met.

Diagnose and recover: to restore the hinge, remove angular alignment while keeping the shoulder seated. The shaft can turn again. For a slider, remove the shoulder condition and retain angular alignment. Choosing a goal alone does not change conditions.

The shoulder condition enforces z = 0; angular alignment enforces θ = 0°. They do not freeze an arbitrary current placement. Removing a condition permits motion without itself moving the component. Angles wrap every 360°.

Model limits: axial travel −30 to +30 mm is a declared lab range, not physical stops. Axis alignment and rigid components are built in. Shoulder seating means ideal plane coincidence, holding z = 0 in both directions; physical shoulder contact alone would not retain a shaft against separation. Contact, collision/interference, friction and load capacity are outside this model. Schematic overlap does not establish a fit or clearance.

In a SOLIDWORKS geometric-mate sequence, concentric alignment followed by shoulder-face coincidence can leave shaft rotation free. This lab's conditions illustrate the resulting motion; they are not a vendor command recorder. Onshape expresses joint motion through mate connectors: Cylindrical permits axial translation and rotation (Tz, Rz), while Revolute permits rotation (Rz). These are not a one-to-one mapping of the SOLIDWORKS steps.

For coupled shaft rotations, continue with Gear Ratios. Diagnose a locked hinge Preserve slider motion

Parallel and perpendicular mates set orientation

Parallel and perpendicular mates set orientation

Parallel keeps selected planes parallel without setting their separation. Perpendicular keeps selected planes at a right angle. Neither condition alone fully locates the part. These diagrams show the planes edge-on.

Distance, angle, and tangent mates control gaps and contact

Distance, angle, and tangent mates control gaps and contact

Distance sets a separation between selected entities. For parallel planar faces, use the normal gap, not a slanted edge length. Angle sets the angle between selected entities; check alignment and direction so the model uses the intended side of the angle.

Tangent keeps compatible curved and planar or curved surfaces touching tangentially. Tangency alone does not enforce rolling without slipping.

Choose a joint or mechanical relationship when motion is the point

Choose a joint or mechanical relationship when motion is the point

For a simple lever on a grounded pin, align the pivot axes and locate the lever axially. Leave rotation free. A hinge mate expresses this single rotational freedom directly. In Onshape, a Revolute mate serves that joint purpose; Cylindrical allows axial slide and spin, Slider allows one translation, and Fastened allows no relative motion. Mate connectors establish the joint frames.

A slot mate locates a pin or similar feature relative to a slot. Select free travel or a prescribed position to match the design; other motions depend on the selections and remaining mates. Onshape's Pin Slot mate allows rotation about the connector's Z axis and translation along its X axis. Set appropriate travel limits; it is not an identical set of SOLIDWORKS slot options.

A gear mate or gear relation couples rotations by a ratio. Locate the shafts first. The relation does not create teeth or prove they mesh without interference. Use Gear Ratios for the ratio calculation and Torque for the separate question of turning effort.

Supporting detail: Addendum 57 — Compare vendor joint vocabulary.

Build reusable parts and subassemblies with deliberate dependencies; Practice

Build reusable parts and subassemblies with deliberate dependencies

Bottom-up design starts with existing parts and brings them into an assembly. Top-down design starts with an overall layout or shared design references and develops parts around them. A mixed approach is common: use a shared layout for custom plates and insert purchased hardware.

A subassembly groups parts into a reusable unit. Give it a useful function, such as a pivot cartridge, rather than hiding unrelated parts in it. Check whether its internal joints are allowed to move at the parent level; a rigid subassembly can make a working joint appear locked.

Top-down references can keep mating holes aligned when the layout changes, but they also create dependencies. Keep the direction of those dependencies understandable and check them when copying or sharing the design.

Supporting detail: Addendum 58 — What makes a feature top-down?.

Use SOLIDWORKS Toolbox or Onshape Standard Content, where available, for standard hardware. Choose the standard, size, thread pitch, length, and material or grade deliberately. A visually similar bolt or an automatic size suggestion is not a completed fastener selection.

Supporting detail: Addendum 59 — Library hardware still needs checking.

For sketching and part-modeling topics, browse Engineering Graphics and CAD. Continue with Checking CAD Assemblies and Exploded Views and Bills of Materials.

Practice shaft freedom Choose locating mates

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies

Checking CAD Assemblies

Diagnose mate errors, inspect overlap and clearance, and test the intended motion before trusting an assembly model.

Judge remaining motion against the design intent

Judge remaining motion against the design intent

A successful rebuild means the CAD system can solve the model. It does not mean the model describes the mechanism you intended. Try moving each component and name the motion that should remain.

Under-mated means freedom remains. That is a defect for a loose cover, but rotation at a lever pivot can be intentional. Over-mated or conflicting constraints ask for relationships that the solver cannot satisfy together. A redundant constraint repeats an existing condition; it adds no useful location and can complicate diagnosis.

For a shaft with concentric axes and seated shoulder faces, one rotation remains. Adding another mate that merely keeps those axes parallel is redundant. Adding an angle mate to lock that remaining rotation may be correct for a stationary shaft and wrong for a rotating lever. Review Assembly Files and Mates for the geometry.

Repair the cause of a mate error before adding more mates; Checklist

Repair the cause of a mate error before adding more mates

  • Read the reported mate error and identify the first failed relationship, rather than only the later errors it causes.
  • Check which component is grounded and whether a moving part was fixed accidentally.
  • Inspect selected faces and axes, alignment direction, offsets, and angle values.
  • Check whether an edit removed or replaced the geometry used by a mate.
  • Temporarily suppress a suspect mate to isolate the conflict, then repair or remove the unnecessary relationship.
  • Rebuild and test motion again, including motion inside subassemblies at the parent level.

Do not force incompatible hole locations together by adding duplicate constraints. Determine whether the parts, the chosen references, or the intended fit are wrong.

Check interference and clearance as different questions

Check interference and clearance as different questions
