Interference is shared volume: two solid parts occupy the same space. Clearance is the gap between parts. A model with no overlap may still lack enough room for movement, manufacturing variation, or tool access.

Run interference detection on the relevant components in the intended configuration and position. Inspect each result. An intentional press fit or simplified thread representation can produce overlap, but an unwanted bolt tip inside a moving path needs attention. Record the reason for any accepted interference.

Supporting detail: Addendum 60 — Selection scope can hide an interference.

Move the mechanism through its intended range; Checklist; Practice

Move the mechanism through its intended range

Move the input joint slowly and watch the connected parts. Test intermediate positions as well as endpoints: a lever can clear a housing at both ends and strike it halfway through. Check which mate limits apply and whether the model passes through solid geometry because collision checking is not active.

A motion preview checks the constraints represented in that preview. It does not automatically prove contact behavior, load capacity, friction, or real-world operation. In particular, a gear relation can drive two rotations even when the modeled teeth do not mesh correctly.

  • Confirm that the input moves and connected parts follow in the expected direction.
  • Inspect travel limits and intermediate positions for collisions and small gaps.
  • Check that the components can be assembled and tools can reach the fasteners.
  • Rebuild after changes and repeat the affected motion and interference checks.
  • Review the final drawing and BOM against the checked assembly.

Supporting detail: Addendum 61 — A joint preview is not always a full-assembly test.

Spot a redundant mate Plan a motion check

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies

Exploded Views and Bills of Materials

Show how components fit together and connect drawing balloons to clear part identities and quantities.

An exploded view separates parts to explain their relationship

An exploded view separates parts to explain their relationship

An assembled view shows the working arrangement. An exploded view spaces components apart so the reader can identify them and follow how they fit. The separation is for communication; it is not an operating clearance or a change to the part geometry.

Separate components along understandable directions, keep related parts aligned, and use explode lines where the connection would otherwise be unclear. Preserve the working assembly and create a saved exploded view rather than deleting mates to pull the model apart.

Supporting detail: Addendum 62 — Use the saved view in a drawing.

A balloon finds a BOM row; a part number identifies the component

A balloon finds a BOM row; a part number identifies the component

A bill of materials (BOM) lists the components required for the stated assembly. A drawing balloon points to a component and usually shows its BOM item number. The item number is a row identifier in that drawing's list. The part number identifies the part for reuse, manufacture, or purchase.

One teaching pivot assembly — quantities per assembly
ItemPart numberDescriptionQuantity
1PV-110Support1
2PV-210Lever1
3PV-310Pivot pin1
4HW-410Thrust washer2
5HW-510Pin retainer1

Balloon 4 identifies HW-410, not four washers. Its quantity is two per assembly. This list has five distinct rows and six component instances. Repeated instances of the same specified part share an item number; different sizes or variants need distinguishable identities.

Supporting detail: Addendum 63 — Linked tables reduce manual mismatches.

Decide whether the BOM lists units or their internal parts

Decide whether the BOM lists units or their internal parts

A top-level list can show a purchased subassembly as one unit. A structured list can show the assembly hierarchy, while a flattened list collects the underlying components without that hierarchy. State the scope before interpreting a quantity. Do not order a complete unit and all its contents accidentally.

Verify part numbers, descriptions, quantities, and relevant configuration or revision information. A library model's filename is not automatically a useful purchasing description. The teaching identifiers above are examples, not an orderable hardware specification.

Supporting detail: Addendum 64 — Subassembly display changes what the table means.

Review the assembly drawing as an identification tool; Checklist; Practice

Review the assembly drawing as an identification tool

  • Show an assembled view that makes the working arrangement understandable.
  • Add an exploded or section view where hidden relationships need explanation.
  • Follow each balloon leader to the correct component and match its number to the BOM.
  • Count repeated components and compare the counts with the stated BOM scope.
  • Check the drawing's design state, units, scale, and necessary assembly notes.

An assembly drawing explains how parts belong together. Individual part drawings supply the manufacturing detail for those parts; do not crowd every part dimension onto an assembly view. See Choosing Drawing Views and the Engineering Graphics and CAD collection for related drawing topics.

Read a balloon Count repeated parts

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication

3D Printing from CAD

Export a solid model, choose how its layers carry load, and inspect the sliced toolpaths before printing.

Build the part by adding layers

Build the part by adding layers

Additive manufacturing makes a shape by adding material. This page uses thermoplastic-filament material extrusion: a printer feeds filament through a heated nozzle and deposits it along paths, much like a controlled hot-glue gun. Fused filament fabrication (FFF) is generic usage for this route; fused deposition modeling (FDM) is a registered trademark of Stratasys.

A slicer divides the model into horizontal cross sections and plans the paths for each layer. The nozzle and build surface move relative to one another to build the next layer. A CAD model describes the desired shape; the sliced file describes how a particular printer will make it.

This page focuses on filament printing. Resin, powder and metal routes use different placement, joining and post-build mechanisms; compare them in Additive Manufacturing Process Families. Their preparation, handling and finishing procedures are not interchangeable.

Export the model, then check its size in the slicer; Checklist

Export the model, then check its size in the slicer

  • Finish and save the editable CAD model. Check that the intended part is a closed solid; see Feature-based Modeling.
  • Export the intended body as STL or 3MF if supported by both programs. Inspect curved surfaces for coarse facets.
  • Import into the slicer and compare a known dimension with the CAD model. Check units, scale, and the number of bodies.
  • Select the actual printer, nozzle, and approved material profile. Do not assume settings imported with a file match the available machine.
  • Orient the part, set walls, infill, layer height, and supports, then slice and inspect the layer preview.
  • Export the printer's required job format using the posted procedure. Save the slicer project so you can revise the setup.

Supporting detail: Addendum 65 — STL and 3MF carry different information.

Use walls for the shell, infill for the interior, and supports where needed

Use walls for the shell, infill for the interior, and supports where needed

Walls, also called perimeters, trace the outside and hole boundaries. Infill fills some of the interior. Solid top and bottom layers close the part. Increasing infill is not a substitute for choosing suitable walls and orientation.

Layer height sets the thickness of each deposited layer. Smaller layers can reduce the steps on sloped surfaces but usually add print time. They do not by themselves make a thin wall or tiny hole printable: nozzle size and extrusion width matter too.

Supports are temporary material beneath regions that cannot print reliably in the chosen orientation. They use material and time, may leave rough contact surfaces, and must be reachable for removal. A short bridge between two supported edges differs from an unsupported overhang; check the machine's demonstrated capability instead of assuming one universal angle limit.

Supporting detail: Addendum 66 — Why more infill does not solve every strength problem.

Orient for load direction, surface quality, and support removal; Practice

Orient for load direction, surface quality, and support removal

Ask which way the part will be pulled or bent. Filament prints are often weaker when a load pulls adjacent layers apart. For a straight bar pulled along its length, laying its length in the build plane is usually a better starting point than printing it upright. Test a representative part before relying on it under load.

Then consider the important faces. A face against the bed takes the bed's texture; a supported underside may need cleanup; a slope shows layer steps. Rotating the part can improve one surface while making another worse. A broad, stable bed contact usually makes the start easier than a narrow footprint.

Practice choosing an orientation

Try it: orient a bracket for support, layer direction and load; Interactive

Try it: orient a bracket for support, layer direction and load

Turn an L-bracket on the build plate and read three consequences together: which downward faces would need support, whether the load in use runs parallel to the layers or must cross the bonds between them, and how layer height leaves steps on the curved faces.

Challenge: this bracket will be screwed to a wall and carry a weight hanging from its arm. Which way up should it print? Read three consequences together: overhangs that need support, the direction of the load relative to the layers, and the steps that layers leave on curved faces.

The bracket: arm 60 mm, back plate 50 mm, both 8 mm thick and 30 mm wide, a 10 mm inner fillet with a concentric 18 mm outer round, and a 6 mm gusset across the inside corner. These are chosen illustrative dimensions.

  • Needs support: downward and flatter than the threshold
  • Downward but at or steeper than the threshold
  • Resting on the plate, or inside the first layer
  • Upward or vertical: never flagged
  • Stretched path: blue = parallel to layers, red-orange = normal to them
Two orientations of the same bracket, 0.20 mm layers, 45° threshold, hanging weight
OrientationUnsupported overhang (projected)On the plateHeight · layersLoad-to-layer angle (max)
A. Arm flat on the plate329 mm²1,260 mm²50.0 mm · 25090° (hanging weight)
B. On its side428 mm²768 mm²30.0 mm · 1500° (hanging weight)

What the comparison shows: standing up (A), the bend's stretched path must turn through the layer stack, so part of it pulls layers apart, and the lower outer round needs support. On its side (B), the stretched path lies within the layers and the curves print as vertical walls, but the gusset now overhangs the open corner. Neither is free: you choose which consequence to accept, or change the design (for example a chamfer instead of a downward-facing round, or no gusset).

Layer steps on a curved face

How the numbers are worked out

  • Build direction: +z, from the plate toward later layers. Layers are horizontal planes.
  • Face inclination θ = arccos|nz| from the horizontal plate (0° horizontal, 90° vertical), where n is the face's outward unit normal. A face is downward when nz < 0.
  • Needs support when downward and θ is less than the threshold (45° here; 44° is flagged, 46° and exactly 45° are not). A face resting on the plate, or lying wholly within the first layer, is supported by the plate. Upward and vertical faces are never flagged.
  • Unsupported-overhang proxy As = Σ Ai·|nz,i| over flagged faces: their area projected onto the plate. Example A: the outer round is flagged from 30 × (18 sin 45° − 18 sin 5.6°) ≈ 329 mm² (the lowest facet sits inside the first layer).
  • Layers N = ⌈H ÷ h⌉. Example A: ⌈50 ÷ 0.20⌉ = 250.
  • Load-to-layer angle φ = arcsin|dz| for the stretched direction d: 0° lies within the layers; 90° is normal to them and must cross the bonds between layers. Within a layer, the slicer also chooses the road (raster) direction; this model does not include it.
  • Layer steps: each layer is the cut at its mid-height, extruded straight up through the layer. The figure measures the largest gap between that stepped outline and the CAD curve in one vertical cut.

Model limits: a geometric teaching model, not a slicer. The support figure is a projected-area proxy: it is not support volume, print time or a promise that a face will print. Bridging between two supported edges, support landing on the part, interface gaps, cooling and removal are not modelled. The 45° threshold is an adjustable guideline, not a universal limit. The load angle is a direction only: no strength value, failure prediction or material data.

Supporting detail: Addendum 67 — Where the threshold and the load rule come from.

Use the preview and the failed part to find the next check

Use the preview and the failed part to find the next check

Missing thin feature
Inspect the sliced paths. A feature visible in CAD may be too thin for the selected extrusion width; revise the feature or an approved setup.
Loose first layer or lifted corners
Check bed preparation, first-layer setup, and the material profile against the machine procedure. Warping involves shrinkage as the part cools.
Sagging underside
Check the orientation, unsupported spans, and support placement before repeating the same job.
Gaps, strings, or shifted layers
Check material condition, extrusion, temperature/profile, and machine motion as appropriate. These symptoms have several possible causes; change one justified factor at a time and record the result.

In the preview, inspect the first layer, small holes, supports, and the final top layers. Estimate time and material before starting. Follow Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping for operation and handling; the nozzle and build surface may remain hot after motion stops.

For parts that must fit together, continue to Choosing a Fabrication Process and Tolerances and Fits.

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication

Choosing a Fabrication Process

Match geometry, load, surfaces, and fit to filament printing or laser-cut sheet construction.

Choose from the required shape and material first

Choose from the required shape and material first

Start with what the part must do. A process is useful only if it can produce the geometry in a suitable material with the required performance.

Filament printing
Builds three-dimensional shapes in layers. It suits changing cross sections, bosses, and internal features when those features can be printed and supports can be removed. Layer direction and service temperature affect the choice.
Laser-cut sheet
Produces planar profiles from a sheet of existing thickness. It suits flat panels, plates, and repeated outlines. Three-dimensional structures need joints, stacked layers, or another forming operation.

A flat nameplate with surface lettering is a natural laser candidate if the sheet is approved. A one-piece curved knob with a raised boss is a natural printing candidate if a suitable printable material meets the load and temperature requirements. Neither choice establishes production time without a job estimate.

For setup details, use 3D Printing from CAD and Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD.

Design features the selected process can actually make

Design features the selected process can actually make

Printed walls and holes
Check that the slicer generates the intended paths. Leave access for support removal. Do not assume a CAD hole prints at its nominal size; measure a representative sample.
Laser-cut webs and corners
Leave enough material between cuts for the part to survive fabrication and use. Account for kerf and heat effects. An infinitely sharp CAD corner does not guarantee an infinitely sharp cut corner.
Sheet joints
Design slots from measured sheet thickness and the intended clearance. Kerf compensation controls the cut edge; clearance controls how two finished parts fit. They solve different problems.
Assembly
Plan how pieces enter their final position and how they are held. A collision-free CAD assembly does not prove that real parts will fit or can be assembled; see Assembly Files and Mates.

Supporting detail: Addendum 68 — Why there is no universal minimum wall or perfect press-fit allowance.

Test the critical feature before making the full part; Checklist; Practice

Test the critical feature before making the full part

  • State the required shape, material, load direction, surface, and fit.
  • Identify the feature most likely to fail: a thin wall, loaded layer joint, supported surface, or mating slot.
  • Make an approved small sample that preserves that feature and the intended process setup.
  • Measure or test the sample against the requirement. Record the setup and the result.
  • Revise the design or setup, then compare time, material, cleanup, and assembly effort before making the full part.

Practice selecting a process Practice clearance and kerf

Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication

Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD

Separate cutting paths from engraved areas, preserve scale, and account for the material removed by the laser.

Use vector paths for outlines and raster scans for filled marks; Practice

Use vector paths for outlines and raster scans for filled marks

A vector operation follows lines and curves. A raster operation scans across an area to make a surface image or filled mark.

A vector path can cut through a sheet or make a shallow score, depending on the material and settings. Raster engraving typically changes the surface without cutting out the part. A bitmap picture of an outline is not automatically a usable vector cutting path.

Practice choosing cut or engrave

Prepare a full-size profile and assign each operation deliberately; Checklist

Prepare a full-size profile and assign each operation deliberately

  • From CAD, export the intended planar face or sketch as a supported vector format such as DXF. View the face normal to its plane; a perspective picture is not a true-size profile.
  • In the vector editor, set units and page/piece size. Import the file and measure a known feature to confirm 1:1 scale.
  • Remove unwanted dimensions, notes, borders, and duplicate paths from the fabrication copy. Check for gaps in outlines that should be closed.
  • Assign cut paths, score paths if used, and raster areas to the correct operations. Inspect fills as well as strokes.
  • Match page/piece size and placement in the artwork and machine software. Preview the job and check its extent against the actual sheet.

CorelDraw is one possible vector editor. Line weight and color can tell a particular driver how to treat an object, but those conventions are not universal. Follow the posted procedure for that driver and confirm the operation in its preview.

Supporting detail: Addendum 69 — Why a hairline is a workflow setting, not a cutting guarantee.

Offset the path toward the waste by half the kerf; Practice

Offset the path toward the waste by half the kerf

Kerf is the width of material removed by a cut. In the simple model below, the laser follows the center of a constant-width kerf. Half the removed width lies on each side of the path.

For an outside part boundary, move the path outward by kerf / 2. For an opening, move the path inward toward the material being removed. Without compensation, a cutout part becomes smaller and a hole becomes larger.

For a desired outside width W, the path-to-path width is W + k, where k is kerf. For a desired opening width H, it is H − k. These are whole-width changes; the offset at each edge is only k / 2.

Measure a test cut in the same material and setup. Kerf can vary with thickness, focus, and settings, and cut edges may taper. If software already compensates the path, do not apply the same allowance again. See Tolerances and Fits for fit requirements.

Practice an outside dimension Practice an opening

Treat power, speed, and pulse settings as a matched setup

Treat power, speed, and pulse settings as a matched setup

Power controls laser output; speed controls how quickly the spot travels. With other conditions held fixed, higher power or slower travel generally puts more energy into a length of cut. That can also increase scorching or melting rather than improve the edge.

Frequency or pulse settings control how pulses are delivered. Controls may use pulses per second, pulses per distance, or a machine-specific scale; read the manual's definition. A percentage from one machine is not a transferable recipe for another.

Use the posted procedure and the manufacturer's starting settings for the exact machine, material, and thickness. Confirm the result on an approved test piece. Check that the cut separates and that engraving is readable before running the complete job.

Supporting detail: Addendum 70 — Manufacturer guidance for selecting a starting setup.

Confirm the material and stay with the operating laser

Confirm the material and stay with the operating laser

Only process materials approved for that machine. Suitable grades of wood and acrylic are common CO₂-laser examples, but coatings, adhesives, thickness, and machine capability matter. A material that can be marked is not necessarily one the machine can cut through.

Do not cut or engrave PVC or vinyl containing PVC. Do not guess the identity of an unknown plastic. Never leave an operating laser unattended. Use the required extraction and follow the machine procedure for a flare-up or other abnormal condition.

Use Equipment Operating Procedure, Fire Safety, and Personal Protective Equipment for the shared safety rules.

Supporting detail: Addendum 71 — Manufacturer safety reference.

Supporting detail

Addendum

Additional evidence, standards context, and background referenced from the main text.

  1. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Auxiliary and Detail Views

    Addendum 1. When one auxiliary view is not enough

    An oblique face is inclined to all three principal projection planes. It is not seen on edge in any of them. An initial auxiliary view can establish an edge view, followed by a secondary auxiliary view showing true shape. That two-stage construction is different from the primary construction below.

    Back to reference 1

  2. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Auxiliary and Detail Views

    Addendum 2. Vendor help and dimensioning references

    See SOLIDWORKS derived drawing views, Creating an Auxiliary View (2025), and Break View. Onshape documents Auxiliary view, Detail view, and Break view.

    For formal conventions, consult the current ASME Y14.3 and related standards, using the edition invoked by the drawing or contract. These introductory explanations do not quote clauses. Continue through the Engineering Graphics and CAD collection for dimensioning topics.

    Back to reference 2

  3. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Choosing Drawing Views

    Addendum 3. Why more pictures do not automatically mean more information

    Repeated information takes space and creates more places for a revision to disagree. A useful additional view makes something clearer: shape, depth, location, or access to a dimension. A pictorial can help orientation, but it does not automatically replace the views and callouts needed to define the part.

    The historical NASA GSFC manual (1994), §3.1 explicitly permits one or two views when they completely define an object. Its §3.5 describes sections, auxiliary views, and details. This is a useful design principle, not a claim that that manual governs every drawing.

    Back to reference 3

  4. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Engineering Graphics in the Design Process

    Addendum 4. Why the process is a loop

    A model can reveal a space conflict that was hard to see in a sketch. A prototype can reveal a behavior that the model did not predict. These findings can send the team back to the geometry or even to the original concept. Sketches remain useful during refinement; drawings can be drafted before the design is final.

    Back to reference 4

  5. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Engineering Graphics in the Design Process

    Addendum 5. Does every design require a separate drawing?

    Some workflows communicate requirements through an annotated model and associated data. Others use drawings as the controlling documents. Follow the agreed deliverables and identify which information governs. A plain shaded model does not automatically communicate material, tolerances, or approval status.

    Back to reference 5

  6. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/First-Angle and Third-Angle Projection

    Addendum 6. Use the glass box to explain the swap

    In third-angle projection, the viewing plane is between the observer and the object. In first-angle projection, the object is between the observer and the viewing plane. Unfolding those planes places the named views on different sides of the front view.

    The angle names refer to projection quadrants. They do not mean rotating the part by one degree or three degrees, and they do not specify the number of views.

    Compare the primary teaching diagrams in NPTEL's first- and third-angle lesson. Autodesk's drawing documentation also explains how the selected convention controls projected-view placement.

    Back to reference 6

  7. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/First-Angle and Third-Angle Projection

    Addendum 7. A documented U.S. example, with its scope

    The NASA Goddard Engineering Drawing Standards Manual (1994), §3.1, printed p. 25 states: Third-angle orthographic projection shall be used for mechanical engineering drawings. That is a requirement in that manual, not proof that every U.S. drawing uses third-angle. Autodesk's Fusion documentation gives a current software example: its ASME drawing setting uses third-angle projection. Bricsys's projection-type reference likewise identifies third-angle with U.S. practice.

    Back to reference 7

  8. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box

    Addendum 8. Why one view can hide an entire change in shape

    Looking from the front collapses depth. A shallow block and a deep block can have identical front outlines. Looking down on them separates those possibilities. Even three matching outside outlines do not prove that internal holes or recesses are identical; hidden lines, sections, dimensions, and notes still matter.

    NPTEL's projection-method lesson and Autodesk's projection-angle explanation provide another way to compare the conventions.

    Back to reference 8

  9. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Pictorial Sketching

    Addendum 9. Isometric drawing and isometric projection use different scales

    An ordinary isometric drawing lays out axis-parallel lengths at the chosen drawing scale. A geometrically projected isometric view foreshortens all three axes equally. Do not mix an isometric projection scale with ordinary drawing lengths in one sketch. The angle of a drawn edge on the paper is not generally its angle on the part.

    Back to reference 9

  10. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Section Views

    Addendum 10. How the explorer decides what is hatched, and its sources

    Each part is built from boxes and round features with vertical axes. The explorer cuts that solid exactly along the plane: the cut face shown on the 3D part and the hatching in SECTION A–A come from the same computed region, and holes inside it remain gaps. The view then shows the first surface you meet looking in the arrow direction. A line is drawn where that surface changes, and where the cut face meets a surface beyond the plane. In an offset section, the cut faces at the two legs are drawn as one face, with no line at the jog. A half section shows the outside on one side of the center line and the section on the other.

    The conventions follow the U.S. Navy training course Blueprint Reading and Sketching, NAVEDTRA 14040, chapter 3, “Section Views” and its full, offset and half sections (pages 3-6 and 3-7), and Linn-Benton Community College’s open textbook Basic Blueprint Reading, “Sectional Views” (CC BY 4.0). For formal drawings, the edition of ASME Y14.3, Orthographic and Pictorial Views invoked by the drawing governs; the explorer is a reading exercise, not a statement of that standard.

    Back to reference 10

  11. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Section Views

    Addendum 11. Drawing standards and scope

    These are introductory conventions, not clause quotations. The current edition of ASME Y14.3 and related drawing standards governs formal work, subject to the edition invoked by the drawing or contract. Consult that edition for exceptions and exact line requirements. Do not identify a material solely from generic diagonal hatching.

    Back to reference 11

  12. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Section Views

    Addendum 12. Vendor help for the drawing tools

    See SOLIDWORKS derived drawing views, Broken-out Section, and Break View. The Removed Section instructions linked here are from the 2022 help edition.

    For Onshape, see Section view, Aligned section view, and Broken-out section view.

    Back to reference 12

  13. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/The Alphabet of Lines

    Addendum 13. Why context matters more than one dash

    Short center marks may look different from long axes, and reduced drawings can make small gaps hard to see. Use a circle, an axis in another view, a section label, or an attached note to confirm the reading. If the supplied drawing is illegible, obtain a readable copy.

    The overlap examples agree with NPTEL's line-precedence explanation. For historical examples of the line families, see the NASA GSFC drawing manual (1994), §3.2.3. These are reading examples, not a replacement for the drafting standard specified on a job.

    Back to reference 13

  14. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Reading Drawings/Visualizing Parts from Multiview Drawings

    Addendum 14. One drawn line can represent several boundaries

    The edge view of a surface can coincide with the outline of another surface. A line is therefore not a unique surface label. Match its endpoints and the surfaces meeting there using another view. The colored areas and heavy highlighted segments here are teaching aids, not extra physical edges.

    Back to reference 14

  15. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Dimensioning/Choosing Dimensions

    Addendum 15. Why nominal arithmetic is not enough

    At the nominal values a closed chain may add up perfectly. Real parts vary within permitted limits, so the extra requirement can conflict with otherwise acceptable sizes. Changing one value also risks leaving its duplicate unchanged. The theory belongs in Tolerances and Fits.

    Back to reference 15

  16. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Dimensioning/Dimension Anatomy and Placement

    Addendum 16. Which parts are standards, and which are layout guides?

    ASME Y14.5 governs dimensioning conventions; its spacing guidance allows for legibility and reproduction. The current edition governs new ASME work unless the drawing or contract specifies another edition. ASME currently lists Y14.5-2018 (R2024). These pages explain conventions in plain words rather than reproducing the standard. For an existing drawing, read its stated standard and revision.

    Back to reference 16

  17. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Dimensioning/Dimension Anatomy and Placement

    Addendum 17. Why older drawings may look different

    Aligned text rotates with the dimension line. You may meet it on older drawings and in other drafting systems. “Old” and “new” alone are not enough to identify the applicable rule. These examples use the ordinary ASME orthographic convention; specialized coordinate dimensioning has additional presentation rules.

    Back to reference 17

  18. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Dimensioning/Hole and Feature Callouts

    Addendum 18. Reading old and new symbol styles

    Legacy notes may say .30 DIA, .55 DP, C'BORE, C'SINK or SP FACE. Modern symbol notation moves that meaning into the symbols shown above. A through hole may be clear from the drawing without THRU, but an isolated diameter value does not prove a through condition. Read the views and notes together.

    Use the standard and edition named on the drawing. The current ASME edition governs new ASME work unless another edition is specified; the ASME catalog lists Y14.5-2018 (R2024). A reference sheet headed “current 2009” is historical, not evidence of today’s edition. Surface finish requirements are a separate language: see Surface Texture and Finish.

    Back to reference 18

  19. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Certification Preparation

    Addendum 19. Why matching mass does not prove the shape is right

    Different shapes can have the same volume and density, and therefore the same mass. A missing cut and extra material removed elsewhere can cancel numerically. Treat mass as one independent check alongside dimensions, feature locations, and drawing views.

    Back to reference 19

  20. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Files and Documents

    Addendum 20. Vendor help for the document model

    Onshape Documents describes the container and its contents. Interface layout and available tools can vary by platform.

    Back to reference 20

  21. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Files and Documents

    Addendum 21. Template and unit references

    See SOLIDWORKS file locations and template types and Onshape account preferences. Changing an Onshape account unit preference does not retroactively change existing documents.

    Back to reference 21

  22. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Files and Documents

    Addendum 22. Why a folder copy needs checking

    A component may live outside the folder you copied. SOLIDWORKS File Utilities describes Pack and Go and tools that update references when files move or change names.

    Back to reference 22

  23. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Files and Documents

    Addendum 23. Why this lab does not imitate a folder copy

    A plain folder copy can omit a component stored elsewhere, but real reference resolution is more complicated than matching visible filenames. This local in-memory lesson predicts a declared graph only. It does not claim that copying these names would repair a real design, and it does not model Onshape documents, cloud permissions, or PDM-managed identities.

    Back to reference 23

  24. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD History, Versions, and Sharing

    Addendum 24. Rollback follows the regeneration sequence

    SOLIDWORKS Rollback Bar help explains moving through the feature sequence. A file can be saved with its bar rolled back, so inspect the bar's position when reopening a model.

    Back to reference 24

  25. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD History, Versions, and Sharing

    Addendum 25. Viewing history, restoring, and branching serve different purposes

    Viewing an earlier state is inspection. Restoring changes a workspace back to an earlier state. Branching gives you a separate place to continue editing. Check the active workspace before any restore or merge. See Onshape Versions and History and Document Management.

    Back to reference 25

  26. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Model Views and Checks

    Addendum 26. Viewing direction is separate from drawing layout

    A standard view tells you where you look from. First-angle or third-angle projection tells you where that view belongs on a drawing sheet. Explore the geometry in Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box. An angled model view is useful for recognizing shape but is not a substitute for dimensions.

    Back to reference 26

  27. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Model Views and Checks

    Addendum 27. Find the view options in vendor help

    Onshape camera and render options links to navigation and display controls. Current browser controls can separate shading choices from hidden-edge choices; older outlines may list them as combined styles.

    Back to reference 27

  28. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Model Views and Checks

    Addendum 28. Measurement reference

    Onshape Measure Tool describes how results depend on selected entities.

    Back to reference 28

  29. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/CAD Model Views and Checks

    Addendum 29. Material assignment and mass-property help

    See Onshape material assignment, Onshape Mass Properties, and SOLIDWORKS Mass Properties for selection and override controls.

    Back to reference 29

  30. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Creating Drawings from CAD Models

    Addendum 30. Find the commands in your CAD version

    Start with the vendor's Onshape drawing help or SOLIDWORKS Help, selecting your installed release where applicable. Consult its drawing creation, projected view, dimension, and update topics. Command sequences are intentionally kept generic here.

    Back to reference 30

  31. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Extrude and Revolve

    Addendum 31. Closed profiles, thin features, and surfaces

    Closed regions are the simplest starting point for solids. Open sketches can be used with thin-feature or surface options, but those are different constructions: a surface has no solid volume, while a thin feature adds a wall thickness. Check the result type before accepting the preview. See Onshape: Extrude.

    Back to reference 31

  32. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Extrude and Revolve

    Addendum 32. Vendor help for extrusion boundaries

    See SOLIDWORKS: Extrude PropertyManager and Onshape: Extrude. A failed up-to feature may indicate that its target no longer covers the profile, not that the sketch is wrong.

    Back to reference 32

  33. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Extrude and Revolve

    Addendum 33. Check overlap and axis selection before adding complexity

    A section that crosses the axis, overlaps itself during rotation, or creates zero-thickness contact can fail. Simplify the section, verify its closure and axis, and inspect a small-angle preview. For the command entry points see SOLIDWORKS: Sketching with Extruded or Revolved Bosses/Bases. A turned part may suggest a revolve, but CAD history does not specify a lathe process; see Lathe Operations.

    Back to reference 33

  34. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Feature-based Modeling

    Addendum 34. Why a small edit can break a later feature

    A face or edge can disappear when the shape changes. A sketch attached to that face, or a fillet attached to that edge, then has a missing reference. Repair the first failed feature before chasing errors farther down the tree. Reordering is constrained by dependencies: a feature cannot use geometry that has not yet been created.

    Back to reference 34

  35. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Feature-based Modeling

    Addendum 35. Vendor help for history and rollback

    See SOLIDWORKS: Rollback Bar, Suppress and Unsuppress Features, and Onshape: Feature and Part Lists. Onshape document history records editing activity; moving a Part Studio rollback bar is not restoring an older document version.

    Back to reference 35

  36. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Feature-based Modeling

    Addendum 36. Fewest features is not always the best model

    A single complicated sketch can hide many unrelated decisions. Several named features may be easier to edit. Count features only after stating which operations are allowed and what the model must do when changed. A feature tree is also not a manufacturing operation sheet: a CAD cut does not specify tooling or setups.

    Back to reference 36

  37. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Feature-based Modeling

    Addendum 37. Mass properties are a check, not proof of a correct part

    Different shapes can have the same volume and mass. Check the geometry as well. Onshape omits parts without assigned material from density-based calculations; inspect its notices and selection. See Onshape: Mass Properties Tool and SOLIDWORKS: Bodies and Features of Multibody Parts.

    Back to reference 37

  38. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Fully Defined Sketches and Design Intent

    Addendum 38. Why subtracting one per relation gives wrong answers

    Coinciding a free point with a fixed point supplies two coordinate conditions. Putting a free point on a fixed line supplies only one. A repeated rule may supply no new independent condition. These counts assume ordinary, nondegenerate geometry: nonzero line lengths and positive radii. At special configurations, independent equations and usable motion require more care; do not assign a universal DOF reduction to each icon.

    Back to reference 38

  39. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Fully Defined Sketches and Design Intent

    Addendum 39. Software treatment of redundant dimensions

    SOLIDWORKS can make a redundant dimension driven; its geometry-status help describes the driven dimension as gray. Onshape's Dimension tool distinguishes driving from driven dimensions and documents the automatic conversion. See Sketch Geometry Status and Onshape: Dimension.

    Back to reference 39

  40. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Fully Defined Sketches and Design Intent

    Addendum 40. Current vendor references for status colors

    SOLIDWORKS: Sketch Geometry Status distinguishes several error states. Onshape: Troubleshooting Sketch Geometry documents geometry and constraint-icon colors. These are editing-state conventions, not a universal color code for every CAD display.

    Back to reference 40

  41. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Fully Defined Sketches and Design Intent

    Addendum 41. Redundancy is not the same as contradiction

    A repeated condition may agree mathematically yet be rejected as a second driving control. Some redundant geometric relations are tolerated: SOLIDWORKS documents a redundant perpendicular relation that leaves a sketch fully defined. Do not assume that every extra icon causes an error. See SOLIDWORKS: FAQ Sketch Relations and Onshape: Working with Constraints.

    Back to reference 41

  42. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Geometric Relations in Sketches

    Addendum 42. Point selection and vendor names

    See Onshape's Coincident and Midpoint. SOLIDWORKS also lists Merge Points for combining sketch points or endpoints in its relation reference.

    Back to reference 42

  43. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Geometric Relations in Sketches

    Addendum 43. Why horizontal plus vertical can already supply a right angle

    A horizontal line and a vertical line already have perpendicular directions. Adding a 90-degree driving dimension can duplicate the existing control. Check the stored rules first. See Onshape: Working with Constraints.

    Back to reference 43

  44. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Geometric Relations in Sketches

    Addendum 44. Check the circular relation definitions

    See Onshape's Concentric and Equal. The SOLIDWORKS 2025 relation table correctly places the coradial definition; the 2026 table misplaces its center-and-radius sentence under Perpendicular.

    Back to reference 44

  45. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Geometric Relations in Sketches

    Addendum 45. Vendor help for tangent and fixed geometry

    Read Onshape: Tangent, Onshape: Fix, and the Fix row in SOLIDWORKS: Description of Sketch Relations.

    Back to reference 45

  46. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Geometric Relations in Sketches

    Addendum 46. Automatic behavior depends on the tool and settings

    Checked against SOLIDWORKS 2026: Using Automatic Relations and Onshape: Automatic Inferencing. The keys differ between programs.

    Back to reference 46

  47. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Patterns, Mirror, and Applied Features

    Addendum 47. Copied geometry and recalculated end conditions can differ

    Onshape feature patterns have a Reapply features option for regenerating the seed's dependencies and end conditions at each instance. A seed that ends at a sloping face may need different geometry at each copy. Do not assume every pattern automatically recalculates that boundary. See Linear Pattern and Circular Pattern.

    Back to reference 47

  48. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Patterns, Mirror, and Applied Features

    Addendum 48. Hole options depend on type and software version

    Use the preview and parameter descriptions instead of assuming every hole has the same options. See SOLIDWORKS: Hole Wizard Type PropertyManager and Hole Wizard Overview. Standard names in a menu do not replace checking the specified hole requirements.

    Back to reference 48

  49. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Sketch Entities and Planes

    Addendum 49. Sketch placement in Onshape

    Onshape creates sketches in a Part Studio and lets you choose a plane, a planar part face, or a mate connector that supplies a coordinate system. This page uses ordinary planes and faces. See Onshape: Sketch Basics.

    Back to reference 49

  50. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Sketch Entities and Planes

    Addendum 50. Find the tools by their software names

    Onshape names include Line, Corner rectangle, Center point rectangle, Center point circle, 3 point circle, Tangent arc, 3 point arc, Spline, Point, and Construction. Its Slot tool builds around selected sketch curves. See Sketch Tools and Slot. These names describe ways to create geometry, not different rules for constraining it.

    Back to reference 50

  51. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Sketch Entities and Planes

    Addendum 51. Vendor reference for construction geometry

    Onshape: Construction explains the reference-only role. SOLIDWORKS: Construction Geometry describes centerlines and converting sketch entities.

    Back to reference 51

  52. Engineering Graphics and CAD/CAD Modeling/Sweeps and Lofts

    Addendum 52. More profiles do not automatically make a better surface

    Extra sections and guides can introduce unwanted waves or conflicting conditions. Start with the fewest that describe the intended shape, then add a control for a specific problem. Profile and guide rules vary with solid, surface, and thin options. See Onshape: Loft and SOLIDWORKS: Description of Sketch Relations.

    Back to reference 52

  53. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Assembly Files and Mates

    Addendum 53. Definitions, instances, and design changes

    Changing a shared part definition can update several instances. Moving one instance in an assembly changes its placement, not the shape of every copy. A configuration can select a particular variant of a component; record the intended variant when sharing or drawing it.

    Onshape: Sharing and Collaboration explains document access and permissions.

    Back to reference 53

  54. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Assembly Files and Mates

    Addendum 54. Vendor help for renaming and sharing

    SOLIDWORKS: Renaming Components distinguishes display names from file names and explains updating references in closed documents. Saving an open assembly alone does not automatically repair every closed drawing. Availability differs for platform-connected installations.

    SOLIDWORKS: Pack and Go Overview describes collecting related files into a folder or ZIP. Use your installed edition's help for the exact controls.

    Back to reference 54

  55. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Assembly Files and Mates

    Addendum 55. Check the insertion setting

    SOLIDWORKS: Insert Components documents the Fix / Float choices. Grounding the base and choosing the remaining joint motion are separate decisions.

    Back to reference 55

  56. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Assembly Files and Mates

    Addendum 56. Why subtracting one DOF per mate gives the wrong answer

    For one free rigid part relative to a grounded part, a planar-face coincident mate leaves three DOF. A cylindrical-axis concentric mate leaves two. Adding a shoulder-face coincident mate perpendicular to that axis removes axial sliding and leaves one rotation. A redundant mate may remove no new freedom. Count the independent motions that survive each step.

    See SOLIDWORKS: Types of Mates for supported selections. These geometric names are not a one-to-one map to Onshape commands.

    Back to reference 56

  57. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Assembly Files and Mates

    Addendum 57. Compare vendor joint vocabulary

    Onshape: Mates describes joint motion through mate connectors. SOLIDWORKS: Machine Design Tools introduces mechanical mates. SOLIDWORKS slot settings distinguish free, centered, distance, and percentage positions.

    Back to reference 57

  58. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Assembly Files and Mates

    Addendum 58. What makes a feature top-down?

    SOLIDWORKS: Top-Down Design explains how layout or other-component geometry controls a feature and creates external references. Merely editing a part while an assembly is visible does not by itself establish that dependency.

    Back to reference 58

  59. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Assembly Files and Mates

    Addendum 59. Library hardware still needs checking

    Onshape: Standard Content explains insertion and sizing. SOLIDWORKS Toolbox is an add-in described in its machine-design overview. Check the resulting model and BOM properties rather than modeling every thread from scratch.

    Back to reference 59

  60. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Checking CAD Assemblies

    Addendum 60. Selection scope can hide an interference

    SOLIDWORKS: Interference Detection describes overlap volumes and options affecting subassemblies and ignored results. Onshape: Interference Detection includes options for standard content and internal subassembly checks. Include the parts you mean to test.

    Back to reference 60

  61. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Checking CAD Assemblies

    Addendum 61. A joint preview is not always a full-assembly test

    Onshape: Mates distinguishes the mate-dialog preview, which can ignore other mates, from assembly animation. Use a whole-assembly check to assess the connected mechanism.

    Back to reference 61

  62. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Exploded Views and Bills of Materials

    Addendum 62. Use the saved view in a drawing

    Onshape: Exploded Views describes saved explode steps and selecting the result in a drawing. An exploded presentation does not demonstrate that the parts can physically be installed in that order; check access separately.

    Back to reference 62

  63. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Exploded Views and Bills of Materials

    Addendum 63. Linked tables reduce manual mismatches

    Onshape: BOM Table describes inserting the assembly's BOM and using balloons to pull its identifiers. Keep the drawing, table, and view tied to the same intended design state.

    Back to reference 63

  64. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Assemblies/Exploded Views and Bills of Materials

    Addendum 64. Subassembly display changes what the table means

    Onshape: Bill of Materials documents structured and flattened views and subassembly BOM behavior. A hidden or excluded row can change what the reader sees, so review the table's scope instead of trusting a row count alone.

    Back to reference 64

  65. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication/3D Printing from CAD

    Addendum 65. STL and 3MF carry different information

    STL represents the surface with triangles and does not record a unit of length. A 3MF file can carry units and multiple objects; a slicer's 3MF project can also carry settings. Support for those extra settings varies between applications. Neither filename alone proves a job is ready for your printer. Prusa documents saving projects as 3MF and its supported file formats.

    Back to reference 65

  66. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication/3D Printing from CAD

    Addendum 66. Why more infill does not solve every strength problem

    Material near the outside can be especially useful when resisting bending. Infill also supports top surfaces and can help resist compression. The useful balance depends on the load and shape. Prusa's infill guidance discusses these different roles.

    Back to reference 66

  67. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication/3D Printing from CAD

    Addendum 67. Where the threshold and the load rule come from

    PrusaSlicer's overhang threshold is measured the same way as here: Prusa's support material guide calls it "the most horizontal slope (measured from the horizontal plane) that you can print without support material." Prusa's modeling guide says printers can cleanly print overhangs at "an angle between 45 and 60 degrees, depending on your nozzle diameter and settings," and warns that a fillet facing the bed creates a steep overhang. That is why 45° is only a starting value here.

    Ahn and colleagues measured FDM ABS specimens and found that strength depends on the direction of the deposited roads; their first build rule is to "build parts such that tensile loads will be carried axially along the fibers" (S.-H. Ahn et al., Anisotropic material properties of fused deposition modeling ABS, Rapid Prototyping Journal 8(4), 2002). The tool shows only the direction; it gives no strength values.

    The build-direction convention follows ISO/ASTM 52900: for planar layer-by-layer processes, the positive z-direction runs normal to the layers, from the first layer to later ones.

    Back to reference 67

  68. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication/Choosing a Fabrication Process

    Addendum 68. Why there is no universal minimum wall or perfect press-fit allowance

    Printer paths depend on nozzle and profile; laser edges depend on the sheet and setup. Material batches and finishing change dimensions too. A small test of the critical feature supplies evidence that a generic dimension cannot. Use Tolerances and Fits to distinguish the intended size from acceptable variation.

    Back to reference 68

  69. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication/Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD

    Addendum 69. Why a hairline is a workflow setting, not a cutting guarantee

    The teaching deck uses hairline strokes for vector cuts and strokes of at least 0.5 pt for raster content. Preserve those values only when the specified driver procedure calls for them. Stroke width alone does not establish cut depth, material suitability, or a safe setting.

    Back to reference 69

  70. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication/Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD

    Addendum 70. Manufacturer guidance for selecting a starting setup

    Epilog's material settings guidance treats its recommendations as starting points. A settings table cannot identify an unknown sheet or replace approval for a material.

    Back to reference 70

  71. Engineering Graphics and CAD/Digital Fabrication/Laser Cutting and Engraving from CAD

    Addendum 71. Manufacturer safety reference

    Epilog's Fire Warning (Fusion Ascent manual, p. 1) states the unattended-operation prohibition and warns that PVC produces toxic and corrosive gases. These are process-specific limits, not a claim about this shop's inventory.

    Back to reference 71
